sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: GitHub Pages feels confusing for one reason: base paths. Once you understand that your site does not live at / but at /your repo/ , every broken deployment you have ever seen suddenly makes sense. This guide is start to finish. It uses real commands, real files, and real verification steps. No shortcuts. No magic. When you finish, you will have a live URL that works, refreshes correctly, and serves assets without 404s. This is not a theory post. It is a lab you can run in any static site project. What GitHub Pages actually is At a high level, GitHub Pages is just a static file host wired directly into your repository. You push a folder of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to a specific branch, and GitHub serves it at a predictable URL. No servers. No containers. No runtime. Just files on disk

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: served over HTTP. At a low level, GitHub Pages does exactly three things. It watches a branch. It copies the files from that branch to its hosting layer. It assigns your repo a URL. Everything else people get stuck on is configuration around paths and build output. The only term that matters is the base path. Your site will live at: https://yourname.github.io/your repo/ If your app thinks it lives at / , every asset will point to the wrong place in production. That is the entire source of the confusion. What you need before touching anything You need a GitHub repository. You need a build command that outputs a static folder. You need to be able to run that build locally without errors. If your local build is broken, GitHub Pages will faithfully publish a broken build. Nothing else is

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: required. No paid services. No API keys. No secret configs. How to deploy from a branch Step 1: Set the base path The first fix is always the same. You tell your project what URL it will live under in production. In most JavaScript static site setups, that is done with a homepage field in package.json . File: package.json Add or confirm: json This one line changes how the build outputs asset URLs. Without it, assets point to /assets/... . With it, assets point to /your repo/assets/... . That is the difference between a working site and a blank page with console errors. Verification: Run a local build: bash npm run build Open the generated index.html inside the build folder. Inspect the and tags. If you see /your repo/ in the paths, the base path is correct. If you still see / , the value

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: is wrong or the build tool did not pick it up. If this step is skipped or wrong, every later step will technically succeed but the deployed site will be broken. Fix the base path first. Always. Step 2: Add a deploy script Once the build folder is correct, you need a repeatable way to publish it. The simplest approach is the gh pages npm package. It pushes a local folder to a remote gh pages branch in your repository. Install it: bash npm install D gh pages Now wire a deploy command. File: package.json Add: json } Replace dist with whatever folder your build actually outputs. Some tools use build , some use public . The command must point to the folder that contains index.html . This script does one thing. It takes your local build output and pushes it to a branch named gh pages . That

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: branch is what GitHub Pages will serve. Verification: Run: bash npm run deploy Expected result: a new branch named gh pages appears in your GitHub repository. If it does, the publishing step worked. If it fails, the error will almost always say the folder does not exist. That means the build output folder name in your script does not match your actual build. Step 3: Turn on GitHub Pages Publishing the branch is not enough. You still need to tell GitHub to serve that branch. Open your repository on GitHub. Go to Settings → Pages. Under Source, select: Deploy from branch Branch: gh pages Folder: / Save. GitHub will now build and host your branch. After a short delay, it will show you the live URL. Verification: Open the URL GitHub provides. The page should load with styling and JavaScript

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: working. Open DevTools → Network. There should be no 404s for CSS or JS files. If you see a blank page or console errors, go back to Step 1. It is almost always the base path. How to deploy with GitHub Actions instead The gh pages branch approach works, but it is not the only way, and it is not the cleanest way anymore. GitHub Pages can also be deployed directly from GitHub Actions. The mental model is different. With Actions based Pages deployments, you do not push files to a gh pages branch. Instead, your workflow builds (or just gathers) a folder of static files, uploads it as a Pages artifact, and GitHub publishes that artifact to your Pages URL. Your repository stays cleaner because your generated site output does not live in your git history. This section is a complete lab for a dead

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: simple static site. It uses a single index.html , an optional styles.css , and a GitHub Actions workflow that deploys on every push to main . Step 0: Make sure Pages is set to "GitHub Actions" Open your repository on GitHub. Go to Settings → Pages. Under "Build and deployment," set the Source to GitHub Actions. If you leave it on "Deploy from a branch," the workflow can run perfectly and you will still sit there wondering why nothing updates. Step 1: Create the simplest possible site In a new repo, create a folder and add index.html . This example is intentionally boring because the point is deployment mechanics, not design. bash mkdir gh pages html demo cd gh pages html demo git init git branch M main git config user.name "Your Name" git config user.email "you@example.com" cat index.html

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: <<'EOF' <!doctype html GitHub Pages HTML Demo GitHub Pages via GitHub Actions This page is deployed from a workflow, not a gh pages branch. document.getElementById("stamp").textContent = "Deployed at: " + new Date().toISOString(); EOF cat styles.css <<'EOF' :root body .wrap h1 p EOF git add . git commit m "Add simple static page" At this point you have a real static site. There is no build step. The folder itself is the deployable artifact. Step 2: Add the GitHub Actions workflow Create this file: .github/workflows/pages.yml yaml name: Deploy Pages on: push: branches: ["main"] permissions: contents: read pages: write id token: write concurrency: group: "pages" cancel in progress: true jobs: deploy: environment: name: github pages url: $ } runs on: ubuntu latest steps: name: Checkout uses:

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: actions/checkout@v4 name: Setup Pages uses: actions/configure pages@v5 name: Upload artifact uses: actions/upload pages artifact@v3 with: path: . name: Deploy id: deployment uses: actions/deploy pages@v4 This workflow is doing four real things. Checkout pulls your repo onto the runner. Configure Pages sets up the Pages deployment context. Upload Pages Artifact packages a folder into the special artifact GitHub Pages expects. Deploy Pages publishes that artifact and returns the live URL as an output. The permissions block matters. Pages deployments require pages: write and id token: write . If you omit them, the workflow can fail with confusing authorization errors even though the YAML “looks right.” The path: . line is intentionally blunt for this demo. It uploads the repository root,

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: which contains index.html and styles.css . In a real app, you would upload the build output directory, like dist or build . Step 3: Push the repo to GitHub Create the repo on GitHub, add the remote, then push. bash git remote add origin https://github.com/ /gh pages html demo.git git push u origin main As soon as the push finishes, the workflow will run. Go to the Actions tab and click the latest run. When it finishes, it will show the deployed Pages URL. Verification: prove it updated Open the deployed URL and refresh twice. You should see the timestamp change. That is your proof that you are not looking at an old cached build and that the workflow is really deploying the current repo contents. If the page loads but CSS is missing, open DevTools → Network and look for a 404 on styles.css

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: . In this plain HTML demo, that almost always means you uploaded the wrong folder, not that Pages is broken. Deploying a built site with Actions Most real projects produce a build folder. The only change you make is what you upload. Instead of uploading path: . , you run your build and upload the build output directory. Example shape: yaml name: Install run: npm ci name: Build run: npm run build name: Upload artifact uses: actions/upload pages artifact@v3 with: path: dist The rest of the workflow stays the same. The only strict rule is that the uploaded folder must contain an index.html at its root. Common Actions based Pages failures Symptom Likely cause Fix Workflow passes, site does not update Pages source still set to “Deploy from a branch” Go to Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: Actions Error: Could not retrieve token Missing id token: write Add it under permissions Error: Failed to create deployment Missing pages: write Add it under permissions 404 on CSS or JS after deploy path points to the wrong folder Confirm it matches your build output Page stays blank Base path mismatch Set homepage or equivalent for your build tool Closing GitHub Pages is not complicated once you respect the base path and the deployment source. Whether you use a gh pages branch or a GitHub Actions workflow, the same rule applies: your build output must know where it will live, and you must confirm the live URL actually serves the files you expect. If you take one thing from this post, take the verification step. Open DevTools. Check for 404s. Refresh until the timestamp proves you are

sourceMaterial.title: github pages deployments confusing
sourceMaterial.content: looking at the new build. That single habit will save you hours of confusion. Keep reading Service Worker Held My Site Hostage: How I Removed It Gatsby Nav Bar Haunted: Fixing a Stuck Dropdown How I Learn by Doing: A Repeatable Mini Project Loop

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: If you run a business in Rockford and you show up in the map pack, you get calls. If you don't, you don't. Google Business Profile is the single highest leverage local SEO task for any business with a physical location or service area. This checklist walks through every field that matters, in the order you should complete it. The short answer Claim or create your Google Business Profile, verify it by postcard or video, pick the most specific primary category you qualify for, fill out every field with accurate information, upload real photos, post updates at least monthly, collect and respond to reviews, and answer questions in the Q&A section. Most Rockford businesses that rank in the local pack have done all of this. Most that don't rank have skipped at least two. Step 1: Claim or create

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: your listing Go to business.google.com and search for your business name. If it already exists, request ownership. If it doesn't, create it. You will need: A Google account (use a shared business email, not a personal one) Your business name exactly as it appears on your signage and website Your real physical address (even if you hide it later as a service area business) A phone number that reaches a human during business hours Verification Google will ask you to verify. The most common methods: Method How it works Timeline Postcard Google mails a card with a 5 digit code to your address 5 14 days Video You record a short video matching your location to Maps 1 5 days Phone Google calls with a code (rare, only for some businesses) Immediate Email Code sent to your business email domain

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: (some businesses) Immediate For Rockford businesses with a storefront, the postcard method is most common. If you are a service area business working out of your home, Google may require video verification. Have your license, utility bill, or equipment with your business name visible. Step 2: Choose your primary category This is the most important field on your entire profile. Google uses it to decide which searches you are eligible for. Pick the most specific category that is accurate. "Plumber" is better than "Contractor." "HVAC contractor" is better than "Home improvement." You can add up to 9 additional categories, but the primary one carries the most weight. Do not add categories you don't actually offer. Google can suspend your listing for miscategorization. Rockford specific tip

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: Search Google Maps for your category in Rockford before you pick. Type "plumber Rockford IL" and see who ranks. Look at their categories to confirm yours matches what Google associates with the map pack for your service. How GBP affects local map pack rankings The map pack (the three businesses shown at the top of local search results with maps and reviews) is driven by three main factors: relevance, distance, and prominence. Your Google Business Profile directly influences all three. Relevance: Your primary category, secondary categories, and the keywords in your description tell Google which searches you are eligible for. A plumber categorized as "Contractor" will not show up for "water heater repair" searches even if that is their main service. Distance: Google considers how far your

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: business is from the searcher. A verified address with accurate service area settings helps Google match you to the right searches. If your service area is wrong, you will show up to the wrong people or not at all. Prominence: This is where reviews, posting frequency, photo updates, and Q&A activity come in. Google treats an active, well maintained profile as a signal that the business is operational and engaged. A profile that has not been updated in a year signals the opposite. The businesses ranking in the Rockford map pack are not there by accident. They have complete profiles, recent reviews, regular posts, and accurate service areas. If your profile is incomplete or stale, you are losing to businesses that simply maintained theirs. Step 3: Fill out every field Google does not

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: penalize you for leaving fields blank, but it does reward you for filling them out. Complete profiles rank better and convert better. Business information Name: Your legal or commonly used name. Do not add keywords like "Rockford Plumber 24/7 Emergency." Google will suspend you for keyword stuffing the name. Address: Your real address. If you are a service area business, you will hide this in the next step. Service area: List the cities and ZIP codes you actually serve. For Rockford, that might include Loves Park, Machesney Park, Belvidere, Cherry Valley, and Rockford proper. Do not list cities you don't serve. Hours: Set your real hours. If you offer 24/7 emergency service, add those as separate hours. Phone: Use your primary business number. This must match your website and every

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: directory listing. See my guide on NAP consistency for why this matters. Description You get 750 characters. Use them. Mention what you do, who you serve, and what makes you different. Do not stuff keywords. Write it like you are talking to a customer. Bad: "Rockford plumber providing plumbing services in Rockford IL for all your plumbing needs." Good: "Family owned plumbing company serving Rockford and the surrounding area since 2012. We handle drain cleaning, water heater installation, repipes, and emergency repairs. Licensed in Illinois. Free estimates on most jobs." Step 4: Add photos Profiles with more photos get more views and more direction requests. Upload: Cover photo: A clean exterior or logo shot Exterior photos: So customers can find you Interior photos: Show your workspace or

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: showroom Team photos: People buy from people Product or work photos: Before and after shots if you do service work Logo: PNG with transparent background Aim for at least 20 photos. Update them quarterly. Google rewards fresh content. Step 5: Enable messaging GBP has a built in chat feature. Turn it on. Customers, especially on mobile, will message you instead of calling. Respond within 24 hours or Google will show a "slow to respond" label. If you can't monitor it, set up auto replies with your phone number and email. But actually responding is better. Step 6: Collect and respond to reviews Reviews are the second biggest ranking factor after your profile completeness and category. You need both quantity and recency. How to get reviews Ask every satisfied customer in person Send a follow up

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: text with your review link Add a review link to your email signature and invoices Do not offer incentives. Google will remove reviews that were paid for. How to respond Respond to every review, positive and negative For positive reviews: thank them and mention something specific For negative reviews: acknowledge the issue, offer to fix it, take it offline Never argue with a reviewer publicly A Rockford HVAC company with 80 reviews and a 4.7 average will outrank one with 12 reviews and a 5.0 average. Volume matters. Step 7: Post updates GBP posts are short updates that show up on your profile. They expire after 6 months but they signal to Google that your profile is active. Post types: What's new: Announcements, seasonal reminders Offers: Discounts, coupons Events: Open houses, workshops

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: Products: Highlight specific services Post at least once a month. Once a week is better. Include a photo and a call to action. Step 8: Answer Q&A Customers can ask questions on your profile. If you don't answer them, anyone can. That includes competitors and random people. Pre seed your Q&A with the questions you get asked most: "Do you offer free estimates?" "What areas do you serve?" "Are you licensed and insured?" "Do you offer emergency service?" Write the question and answer it yourself. This controls the narrative and gives searchers the information they need without calling. Common mistakes I see in Rockford 1. Using a home address as a storefront when you don't see customers there. Use service area settings instead. 2. Keyword stuffing the business name. Google suspends for this.

sourceMaterial.title: google business profile checklist rockford
sourceMaterial.content: 3. No photos. A profile with zero photos looks abandoned. 4. Ignoring reviews. Unanswered negative reviews tell Google and customers you don't care. 5. No posts in 6 months. An inactive profile gets deprioritized. Next steps If you want help setting up or optimizing your Google Business Profile, I offer local SEO services for Rockford area businesses. You can also reach out directly if you have questions about your specific situation.

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: I learn faster by shipping small, real things than by planning large, imaginary ones. This post describes the actual loop I use when I want to understand a tool or idea: I build a tiny working demo, put it somewhere public, then write down exactly what broke and what I changed. Nothing here is aspirational. Every step ends in a file, a command, or a URL you can verify. The point of this loop is not productivity theater. The point is to force contact with real environments: the browser, the build output, the deployment host, and the mistakes that only appear once something is live. The shape of the loop A usable learning loop has three visible artifacts. There is a local project that runs. There is a public link that proves it runs outside your machine. There is a short written note that

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: captures what actually went wrong and what you fixed. If any of those are missing, the loop is not complete and the learning stays fuzzy. Here are the three artifacts that make the loop complete: Local project that runs — a file or repo you can execute on your own machine Public link that proves it runs — a deployed URL anyone can visit (Source) Short written note — a lesson.md capturing what broke and what you fixed This post walks through a concrete example using a single static HTML page. The example is intentionally simple because the mechanics of building, verifying, and deploying are the part that matters. The same loop applies to larger stacks later. A real starting point: one tiny demo Start with an empty folder and create the smallest possible project. No frameworks, no

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: scaffolding tools, no generators. Just a file that does one thing and can be opened in a browser (Source). bash mkdir mini demo cd mini demo cat index.html <<'EOF' <!doctype html Mini Demo Click the box const box = document.getElementById("box"); const status = document.getElementById("status"); box.addEventListener("click", () = ); EOF Open index.html in a browser and click the square. If the timestamp appears, the demo is real. This is the first important point: the project exists outside your head and outside a tutorial. It runs. The demo uses a standard click event listener on a DOM element (Source) and updates text content via textContent (Source). Local verification before anything else Before thinking about deployment, confirm the demo behaves correctly in a clean browser session.

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: Reload the page. Click again. Confirm the timestamp updates every time. If this fails locally, deploying it only publishes a broken artifact. Fix local behavior first, always. Here is a quick local verification checklist: 1. Open index.html in a fresh browser tab (not a cached session) 2. Click the square and confirm the timestamp appears 3. Reload the page (hard refresh: Cmd+Shift+R or Ctrl+Shift+R) and click again 4. Confirm the timestamp updates on every click — if it stays stale, your event listener may not be re attaching 5. Test in a second browser if possible — this catches browser specific quirks early (Source) This step sounds obvious, but it is where most abandoned projects die. Local verification is the first filter that separates "I thought about building" from "I built

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: something that executes." Putting the demo under version control Now make the demo something you can actually share. Initialize a git repository and commit the file (Source). bash git init git branch M main git add index.html git commit m "Add mini demo" At this point you have a reproducible artifact. Anyone can clone the repo and open the same file. That reproducibility is part of the learning process. If you cannot reproduce your own demo later, the learning is lost. Deploying the demo to a real URL A demo that only runs on your machine is still half finished. The moment you put it on a public URL, you force yourself to confront file paths, hosting behavior, and browser caching. This example uses GitHub Pages through GitHub Actions because it removes manual steps and produces a visible

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: deployment log (Source). Create the workflow file: .github/workflows/pages.yml yaml name: Deploy Pages on: push: branches: ["main"] permissions: contents: read pages: write id token: write concurrency: group: "pages" cancel in progress: true jobs: deploy: environment: name: github pages url: $ } runs on: ubuntu latest steps: name: Checkout uses: actions/checkout@v4 name: Setup Pages uses: actions/configure pages@v5 name: Upload artifact uses: actions/upload pages artifact@v3 with: path: . name: Deploy id: deployment uses: actions/deploy pages@v4 This workflow is mechanical. It checks out your repository, tells GitHub this job is a Pages deployment, uploads the current folder as the site artifact, and publishes it (Source). There is no build step because this demo is plain HTML. For larger

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: projects, the only change is adding a build command before the upload. Here is what each workflow step does: Checkout — clones your repo onto the runner using actions/checkout@v4 (Source) Setup Pages — configures the GitHub Pages environment using actions/configure pages@v5 (Source) Upload artifact — packages the current folder as a Pages artifact using actions/upload pages artifact@v3 (Source) Deploy — publishes the artifact to the Pages URL using actions/deploy pages@v4 (Source) Push the repository to GitHub: bash git remote add origin https://github.com/ /mini demo.git git push u origin main When the push completes, open the Actions tab in your repo. You will see the workflow run. When it finishes, GitHub shows the live Pages URL (Source). Open that URL and click the square. If the

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: timestamp updates, your demo is now running on infrastructure you do not control. That is the second important point: your code survived a clean environment and a real host. Proving the deploy actually updated To avoid fooling yourself with cached pages, reload the URL with a hard refresh (Source). Click the square again. The time should change. If the page does not update, check the Actions run logs. They will show whether a new deployment actually happened. This is where you learn to trust logs over assumptions. Writing down the lesson After the demo is live, write one short note about what actually happened. Create a file named lesson.md and write three sentences. bash cat lesson.md <<'EOF' The demo broke the first time because I forgot to enable Pages → Source → GitHub Actions. After

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: fixing that, the workflow deployed correctly and returned a live URL. Next time I will always check Pages settings before debugging YAML. EOF This is not documentation for others. This is a memory aid for you. When you repeat this loop with a different tool later, these small notes prevent you from relearning the same mistakes from scratch. Why this loop works This process forces three real interactions: writing code that runs, deploying to a host you do not control, and reading logs when something fails. Those interactions are where understanding forms. Reading articles or watching videos can introduce concepts, but shipping even a tiny demo is what makes them stick. The learning loop at a glance Stage What you do Artifact produced What it proves 1. Build Create the smallest possible

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: project Local files (e.g. index.html ) Code runs in a browser 2. Verify Reload, click, confirm behavior A passing local test The demo is real, not imagined 3. Version control git init , commit, push A GitHub repo The demo is reproducible 4. Deploy GitHub Actions workflow runs A public Pages URL Code survives a clean host 5. Record Write lesson.md A short note You captured what broke and why Over time the demos get larger, the stacks change, and the deployment targets evolve. The loop stays the same: build something small, verify locally, deploy publicly, record what actually broke. That repetition is the real curriculum. Closing If you have a local demo that runs, a public URL that proves it, and a short note that captures what went wrong, you have learned something concrete. Everything

sourceMaterial.title: how i learn by doing
sourceMaterial.content: else is just preparation for that moment. sourceMaterial.title: interactive portfolios
sourceMaterial.content: Portfolios should be readable first and interactive second. Not because interaction is bad, but because the person viewing your site is usually scanning, not exploring. If the first ten seconds is motion, hidden panels, and clever transitions, you are making your best content harder to access. What I actually mean by "interactive portfolio" is simple. It is a normal portfolio that still works as plain HTML, and then you add one or two small interactions that make it feel alive without hiding the important parts. If you can turn off JavaScript and still understand who you are, what you built, and how to contact you, you are in a good spot. What this guide builds This guide builds one small interactive section the safe way. You will end with a page that scans quickly, still has personality,

sourceMaterial.title: interactive portfolios
sourceMaterial.content: and has an interaction that does not break accessibility or bury your content. Here is the standard I use: a recruiter should be able to answer three questions without clicking anything. Who is this person. What have they built. How do I contact them. If those answers require a toggle, a tab, or a hover effect, the structure is wrong. What counts as "safe" interaction Safe interaction is interaction that adds convenience or flavor, not interaction that gates information. A theme toggle is safe because it does not hide your projects. A "show more details" panel is usually safe if the summary is still visible. A filter for projects can be safe if an "All" view exists and nothing disappears permanently. Unsafe interaction is anything that replaces the readable base. If your Projects section

sourceMaterial.title: interactive portfolios
sourceMaterial.content: is only visible after a tab click, or your contact info is inside an accordion, you are betting your entire portfolio on someone choosing to interact. Most people will not. Build the readable base first Create a folder and make a single HTML file. This is intentionally plain because the whole point is making sure the content is readable without styling or scripts. File: index.html html <!doctype html Bradley Matera Portfolio Skip to content Bradley Matera Systems minded builder. I ship small demos and keep them readable. Projects About Contact Projects These are fast links to real work. Details can come later, but the list has to scan fast. AnimalSounds Small interactive demo focused on clean UI and quick scanning. WebGPU Triangle Demo A minimal graphics demo that proves the project runs

sourceMaterial.title: interactive portfolios
sourceMaterial.content: and renders. About I care about repeatable builds, clear structure, and projects that do not fall apart once they are deployed. I would rather have one clean interaction that works everywhere than five effects that look good only on my machine. Contact Email: bradmatera@gmail.com At this point, open the file in a browser and do one boring check that matters. Hit Tab until the skip link appears, press Enter, and confirm focus jumps into the main content. If the page is readable and the skip link works, the foundation is solid. Add one interaction without hiding core content The safest first interaction is a detail panel that is clearly "extra" and does not contain anything essential. The Projects list stays visible. The interaction simply gives a way to expand optional context. Add this

sourceMaterial.title: interactive portfolios
sourceMaterial.content: section right after the Projects list. html Focus This is optional detail. It should never be required to understand the page. Show focus areas Clear documentation and predictable structure Repeatable deploys and clean build output Accessible UI that still looks intentional const button = document.getElementById("focusToggle"); const list = document.getElementById("focusList"); button.addEventListener("click", () = ); This is the difference between "interaction" and "UI trick." The content exists in the DOM. The button toggles visibility, and the ARIA attributes stay honest so assistive tech understands the state change. Now verify it like a normal person. Click the button. Confirm the list appears. Click again. Confirm it hides. Then hit Tab and confirm the button is reachable by keyboard

sourceMaterial.title: interactive portfolios
sourceMaterial.content: and still works when you activate it. Add minimal styling that improves scanning Most portfolios get worse when styling becomes the main event. Keep the typography and spacing clean first. Effects can wait. File: styles.css css :root body .site header main nav a .lede .projects .projects li .muted .focus button .skip link .skip link:focus Reload the page and do the same scan test again. Can you read the header, see Projects, and see Contact without hunting. That is the actual goal. If it scans clean now, you have permission to add small personality later. The interaction rules I follow When people say "make it interactive," they usually mean "make it feel alive." That is fair. The problem is that most interactive ideas also hide content. The easiest way to avoid that trap is to keep a

sourceMaterial.title: interactive portfolios
sourceMaterial.content: clear boundary between what must be visible and what can be optional. Below is a simple reference table. It is not theory. It is just a way to decide whether an idea is helping or harming the scan experience. Interaction Usually safe Usually risky Why it matters Theme toggle ✅ ❌ Does not hide content, just changes presentation "Show more details" below a summary ✅ ❌ Keeps the scan path intact Project filtering ✅ ⚠️ Safe if an "All" view exists and nothing disappears permanently Hover only reveals ❌ ✅ Hover does not exist on touch devices and often hides important info Tabs for core sections ❌ ✅ Forces clicks to discover basic content Auto animations on load ⚠️ ⚠️ Can be fine, but it can also distract from scanning Accessibility checks that are actually worth doing You do not need a full

sourceMaterial.title: interactive portfolios
sourceMaterial.content: audit to avoid the most common problems. You need a small handful of checks that catch the things people break with interaction. First, keyboard only. Reload the page, do not touch the mouse, and hit Tab through the header links and the toggle button. If the page becomes annoying to use, it will be annoying for more people than you think. Second, reduced motion. If you later add animation, respect prefers reduced motion . If your portfolio depends on motion to communicate structure, you are building a demo of animation, not a portfolio. Third, readability without JavaScript. Turn off scripts or use a browser extension to block them. The Projects list and Contact section must still exist and make sense. The part recruiters actually care about Most reviewers are not judging your animation

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: Job hunting is a pipeline, and pipelines get messy when you try to hold them in your head. The only way I have ever seen it become less chaotic is when you turn it into something you can point at: a tracker you actually update, a place where each resume version lives, and a weekly check that forces you to react to reality instead of vibes. This is a practical workflow you can run locally. It is not a productivity system and it is not a "brand building" post. It is the minimum set of files and habits that make a search measurable. If you do not want structure, stop here. If you do, this is start to finish. What you will end up with By the end, you will have one tracker file that cannot get lost, one folder that keeps resume versions tied to the roles you applied to, and one weekly review

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: note that prevents you from repeating the same week forever. You will also have a simple rule for follow ups so your pipeline does not silently stall. The only standard I care about is this: if someone asked you right now "how many roles have you applied to in the last 30 days and what happened," you could answer in under a minute by opening a file. How I think about the job search High level, the job search is a pipeline: you apply, you wait, you follow up, you either move forward or you do not, and you adjust. Low level, it is just data. Company, role, date applied, status, link, and notes. When you keep that data in a tracker, you start seeing patterns. When you do not, every rejection feels random and every follow up becomes a guess. This workflow is intentionally small. It assumes you

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: are doing the hard parts already: finding roles, tailoring your resume, and applying. The workflow does not replace that work. It makes it visible. What you need You need a folder on your machine for job search artifacts and you need one tracker format. I use CSV because it works everywhere: spreadsheets can open it, scripts can read it, and git can diff it. If you prefer a Google Sheet, you can mirror the same columns there. The key is choosing one place that is "truth." Start to finish Step 1: Create a tracker that you will actually update Make a folder dedicated to the search and create one CSV file inside it. I am using job search/ because it is boring and obvious. If you already have a home for personal admin work, put it there instead, but keep it in one place. bash mkdir p job

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: search cat job search/tracker.csv <<'EOF' company,role,location,date applied,status,source,posting link,follow up date,last touch,notes EOF Those headers are not "nice to have." They prevent the most common problem: writing notes that cannot be compared later. "Source" is where you found it (LinkedIn, Indeed, company site, referral). "Follow up date" is the date you intend to follow up. "Last touch" is the last time you did anything related to that application. That single field stops you from wondering whether you already sent a message. Now add one real row immediately. If you do not do this right now, the tracker becomes a dead file and the whole idea collapses. bash echo "Amazon,Cloud Support Engineer Intern,Seattle WA,2025 05 01,Completed,Amazon jobs,https://example.com,2025 05

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: 08,2025 05 08,Internship pipeline" job search/tracker.csv Replace the values with a real entry from your own search. The point is not the example. The point is that your tracker has at least one real row today. Verification that this step worked is simple. Open the file. If it has headers and at least one real entry, it is alive. Step 2: Make resume versions a file system problem Resumes get messy because you reuse "the one resume" for jobs that are not the same, then you cannot remember what you sent or what changed. The fix is not a new resume. The fix is saving versions that are tied to roles. Create a folder for resume outputs and a folder for the job descriptions you applied to. Saving the job description is not optional if you want to learn. A posting can disappear or change. If you

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: do not keep it, you lose the ability to review what you actually applied to. bash mkdir p job search/resumes mkdir p job search/postings Use a naming convention that bakes in date, company, and role. Keep it boring. Boring scales. Example: job search/resumes/2026 01 29 amazon cloud support.pdf job search/postings/2026 01 29 amazon cloud support.txt If you want a simple command to capture a posting quickly, paste the job description into a text file. bash cat job search/postings/2026 01 29 company role.txt <<'EOF' PASTE THE JOB DESCRIPTION HERE EOF Now connect those files back to your tracker by adding a note in the row like "resume: 2026 01 29 company role.pdf" and "posting saved." It sounds tedious until you realize it makes reviewing outcomes possible. Step 3: Add a weekly review note

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: that forces a change A tracker by itself can still become a graveyard. The weekly review is where it becomes a feedback loop. You are not writing a diary. You are doing a quick operational check: what moved, what stalled, what you will change. Create the weekly notes file. bash cat job search/weekly notes.md <<'EOF' Weekly Job Search Review Week of: What I shipped: What moved forward: What stalled: One change for next week: EOF Now actually fill it in once per week. It can be three lines. The only required field is "One change for next week." If you cannot name one change, you will repeat the same week. Step 4: Follow ups that do not feel weird Most searches die because follow ups never happen, not because the resume is bad. The trick is to make follow up dates part of the tracker, not

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: something you "remember." This is the rule I use because it is predictable and does not turn into spam: If you applied and heard nothing, follow up 5–7 business days later. If you had an interview, follow up within 24 hours with a thank you and then again after the timeframe they gave you passes. That is it. You are not chasing people every two days. You are just keeping your pipeline from freezing. When you add a row to the tracker, set follow up date immediately. That is the whole move. A tracker table that stays readable If you prefer spreadsheets over CSV editing, keep the CSV as the "source of truth" and open it in a spreadsheet app. The format is the same either way. What matters is consistency. Here is the meaning of each column in plain language. Column What it is Why it exists

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: company The company name Lets you group outcomes by employer role The role title Lets you compare role families location City/remote/hybrid Prevents confusion later date applied When you applied Enables 30/60/90 day review status Applied, Phone Screen, Interview, Rejected, Offer, etc Turns feelings into states source Where you found it Shows which sources convert posting link The URL Gives you a quick jump target follow up date When you will follow up Prevents silent stalls last touch Last action you took Prevents duplicate follow ups notes Anything that matters Captures context without bloating the row How you know this workflow is working You will feel it working when you stop wondering what happened and start seeing what happened. You will have a count of active applications. You will

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: have follow ups scheduled. You will be able to look back and see whether a certain resume version or source actually led to interviews. The weird part is that this does not make job hunting easier emotionally. It just makes it less foggy. You can still get rejected. You can still get ignored. The difference is you can now respond with a real change instead of random flailing. Common failure modes If this falls apart, it is almost always one of three things. The tracker exists but never gets updated. That is solved by making "add row to tracker" part of the application process itself. Apply, then log. Same session. Resume versions exist but are scattered. That is solved once: move them into the folder and rename them. You only have to clean the mess once. The weekly note stays empty. That

sourceMaterial.title: job hunting
sourceMaterial.content: is solved by making the weekly note stupidly small. If you cannot write the full template, write one line: "One change next week: ." Keeping the loop alive matters more than writing a nice note. Closing This is not a motivational system. It is a small set of files that turns a job search into a pipeline you can inspect. If you can see the pipeline, you can change it. If you cannot see it, you will keep guessing. If you implement only one part, implement the tracker. A single CSV that stays current beats any complicated setup that never gets touched. sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: NAP consistency is boring. It is also one of the few local SEO tasks that you can fully control, and getting it wrong quietly drags down your rankings for months before you notice. This guide explains what NAP is, why inconsistency hurts, and how to audit and fix your listings without paying a service $300 a year. The short answer NAP stands for Name, Address, and Phone number. It must be identical across every website that lists your business, including Google, Bing, Apple Maps, Yelp, Facebook, and the Better Business Bureau. Inconsistent NAP confuses Google about which listing is correct, which lowers your trust score and drops your local rankings. Audit your listings twice a year, fix any mismatches, and never change your business name, address, or phone without updating every

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: directory. What is NAP? NAP is the three pieces of information that identify your business across the web: Name: Your business name, exactly as registered Address: Your physical location, formatted consistently Phone: Your primary phone number, in the same format everywhere Some directories ask for more (website, hours, categories), but NAP is the core. Google crawls the web looking for your NAP on other sites. Each consistent mention is a vote of confidence. Each inconsistent mention is a contradiction. Why inconsistent NAP hurts rankings Google's local algorithm uses citations as a trust signal. If 30 websites say your business is at "123 Main St, Rockford, IL 61101" with phone "[phone withheld]," Google is confident that is correct. If 5 of those sites say "123 Main Street" and 3 say

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: "[phone withheld] ext 2," Google is less confident. When Google is unsure, it ranks you lower. Not because you are being penalized, but because it would rather show a business it is confident about than one it isn't. Common inconsistency sources 1. You moved and updated Google but not Yelp, Facebook, or the BBB 2. You changed phone numbers when switching to VoIP or Google Voice 3. An old employee created listings with a personal phone number 4. Data aggregators scraped an old version of your info and spread it 5. You used different abbreviations ("St" vs "Street", "IL" vs "Illinois") The abbreviation issue is real. Google does not care about "St" vs "Street" on its own, but if half your citations say one and half say the other, it looks inconsistent. Pick one format and use it everywhere.

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: How to audit your citations Step 1: Write down your canonical NAP Decide on your official format and write it down. Example: Matera Plumbing 456 Industrial Ave Rockford, IL 61109 [phone withheld] Rules: Use the exact legal name or DBA, no keywords added Use the USPS standard address format Pick one phone number and stick with it Do not use tracking numbers in citations (see below) Step 2: Search for your business Search Google for your business name, your phone number, and your old phone numbers. Search in quotes: "Matera Plumbing" "[phone withheld]" "[phone withheld]" "Matera Plumbing" Rockford This will surface most of your existing citations. You can also use free tools like the BrightLocal citation checker, but manual searching catches more. Step 3: Check the major directories Go through each

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: of these and verify your NAP matches: Directory URL Notes Google Business Profile business.google.com Most important Bing Places bingplaces.com Second most important Apple Maps business.apple.com Growing fast Yelp biz.yelp.com Hard to fix, do it first Facebook facebook.com/business Check your page info BBB bbb.org If you are accredited Yellow Pages yellowpages.com Still sends data to others Foursquare foursquare.com Feeds Apple Maps MapQuest mapquest.com Lower priority but free TripAdvisor tripadvisor.com Only if relevant to your industry Step 4: Document the mismatches Create a spreadsheet. Columns: Directory, Current Name, Current Address, Current Phone, Correct Name, Correct Address, Correct Phone, Status. Fill it in as you audit. You will be surprised how many are wrong. Most

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: businesses I audit have 5 10 inconsistencies across the top directories. Step 5: Fix them Go to each directory, claim the listing if you haven't, and update the NAP to match your canonical format. Some directories make this easy. Yelp and Yellow Pages can be stubborn. Be persistent. Tools to manage citations If you have more than 20 citations to manage, manual updates get tedious. These tools help: Tool Cost What it does BrightLocal $39/mo Audit, build, and fix citations Whitespark $27/mo Citation building and cleanup Yext $99/mo Power listings, stops syncing when you cancel Semrush Listing Management Included in Semrush Syncs to major directories I do not recommend Yext for most small businesses. When you cancel, your listings revert to whatever the data aggregators had before. You are

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: renting your citations, not owning them. BrightLocal and Whitespark make permanent changes. For a business with 5 10 citations, do it manually. It takes an afternoon and you own the results. Common mistakes Using a virtual office address This is the most damaging mistake. You rent a virtual office in a better part of town, use that address on your citations, and think you are tricking Google. You are not. Google cross references addresses with street view, other listings, and business registration data. If it detects a virtual office, it suspends your listing. Use your real address. If you are a service area business, hide it on Google but use it consistently on directories that require it. Different phone numbers on different listings Some businesses use a tracking number on Yelp, a

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: different one on their website, and their real number on Google. This is a mess. Google sees three different phone numbers and does not know which is real. Use one phone number everywhere. If you need call tracking, use a service that forwards to your real number and uses call tracking numbers only in specific ad campaigns, not in organic citations. Not updating after a move You moved 2 years ago. You updated Google. You forgot Yelp, Bing, and the BBB. Now Google sees conflicting addresses and your trust score drops. Any time your address or phone changes, update every directory. Use your audit spreadsheet to make sure you don't miss any. How often to audit Twice a year is enough for most businesses. Once a quarter if you are in a competitive market. The audit takes 1 2 hours if you stay

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: on top of it, or a full day if you let it slide for years. Which citation sources actually matter Not all directories carry the same weight. Google's local algorithm trusts some sources more than others, and a handful of platforms feed data to dozens of secondary sites. Here is the priority order I follow when building or cleaning up citations. Tier 1 — must have, do these first: Google Business Profile. This is the single most important citation. It feeds Google Maps, the local pack, and your knowledge panel. Get this perfect before touching anything else. Bing Places. Second most important. Bing still powers a meaningful share of search traffic, and Bing Places data feeds into other Microsoft properties. Apple Maps. Growing fast, especially on mobile. Claim your listing at

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: business.apple.com. Apple pulls data from Foursquare and other aggregators, but claiming directly gives you control. Tier 2 — high priority, do these next: Yelp. Difficult to update and stubborn about changes, which is exactly why you should fix it early. Yelp data also feeds Apple Maps and other directories. Facebook. Your Facebook page NAP shows up in Facebook search and gets scraped by data aggregators. Update the About section, not just the page name. Tier 3 — worth doing but lower impact: Better Business Bureau (if accredited), Yellow Pages , Foursquare , MapQuest , TripAdvisor (if relevant to your industry). The tier 1 sources are where I see the biggest ranking impact. If you only have an afternoon, fix those three and you have covered 80% of the benefit. What happens when NAP is

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: inconsistent I have seen the impact firsthand. A plumbing client in Rockford had their address listed as "456 Industrial Ave" on Google, "456 Industrial Avenue" on Yelp, and "456 Industrial Ave." with a trailing period on Facebook. Same address, three formats. Their local pack ranking sat at position 7 for "plumber Rockford" for six months. After standardizing all three to the exact same USPS formatted string and waiting about five weeks, they moved to position 4. Nothing else changed. No new content, no new backlinks, no new reviews. Just NAP consistency. The customer confusion side is worse than the ranking impact. When Yelp shows an old phone number and a customer calls it, that call goes to whoever has that number now. I have seen businesses lose leads for months because a

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: decommissioned phone number was still live on three directories. The customer thinks the business closed. The business thinks marketing is not working. A step by step NAP cleanup process If you have never audited your citations, here is the exact process I use. 1. Write your canonical NAP. One format, written down. Use the USPS address format. Pick one phone number. No abbreviations that you will not use consistently. 2. Search for every existing mention. Search your business name in quotes, your phone number in multiple formats, and your old phone numbers. Save every URL that mentions your business. 3. Build the audit spreadsheet. Columns: Directory, URL, Current Name, Current Address, Current Phone, Canonical Name, Canonical Address, Canonical Phone, Status (Match / Mismatch / Fixed),

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: Date Fixed. 4. Fix tier 1 first. Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Apple Maps. These have the most ranking impact. 5. Fix tier 2 next. Yelp and Facebook. These are harder to update but worth the effort. 6. Work through tier 3. BBB, Yellow Pages, Foursquare, MapQuest, and any industry specific directories. 7. Re check in 30 days. Some directories revert changes or take time to process updates. Verify that your fixes stuck. How long citation changes take to affect rankings This is the question I get most often, and the honest answer is: it depends, but here are the real timelines I have seen. Google Business Profile changes: Usually reflected in the local pack within 3 7 days. Major changes (address moves, category changes) can take 2 4 weeks and may trigger re verification. Bing Places

sourceMaterial.title: local citations nap consistency
sourceMaterial.content: and Apple Maps: 1 3 weeks for changes to propagate. Yelp and Facebook: 2 4 weeks. Yelp is slower because of their review process for business info changes. Aggregator fed directories (Yellow Pages, Foursquare, MapQuest): 4 8 weeks. These pull from data aggregators like DataAxle and Neustar, which update on their own cycles. Full ranking impact from a complete NAP cleanup: 4 8 weeks after the last directory is fixed. I have seen it happen as fast as 3 weeks and as slow as 10 weeks. The businesses with the most inconsistencies to start with see the biggest improvement. Do not expect overnight results. Citation cleanup is a slow burn, but it is one of the few local SEO efforts that produces a durable, compounding benefit. What to do next If you want help auditing and fixing your citations, I

sourceMaterial.content: A demo is only as honest as its write up. WebGPU is especially easy to oversell (See the WebGPU specification and Chrome's WebGPU documentation.) because most people reading a post cannot tell what is "one triangle" versus "real engine ish work" unless you show them exactly where it lives in code. If you want the post to be credible, every claim needs a file path you can point at and a proof link that still works when someone clicks it six months later. What this audit fixes Unverifiable claims — sentences that describe behavior not present in the repo get cut or rewritten. Broken proof links — every URL in the post is opened and confirmed to resolve. Future work disguised as features — plans are moved into a clearly labeled "Next experiments" section. Missing file references — each

sourceMaterial.title: making triangle webgpu demo match reality
sourceMaterial.content: feature sentence gets a deep link to the implementing file. This post is the audit process I use to make the write up match the repo. It is not about polishing the prose. It is about deleting anything that is not visible in code, labeling future work like future work, and fixing links so a reader can verify everything without guessing. What an honesty audit actually is When you finish this audit, your WebGPU demo post will only say what the repo actually does. Not what you planned, not what you think it does, not what you remember it doing on your machine three weeks ago. The end state is boring in the best way. A reader can open the repo, find the exact lines that back up each statement, and run the demo without stepping on a broken link. That is the whole rule: if a claim is not visible

An honesty audit is just a comparison: what the blog claims versus what the repository proves. High level, you treat the blog like marketing copy that needs receipts. Low level, you open the repo, identify the real behavior, and then rewrite the blog so every sentence can be backed up by a concrete reference. The audit has only three objects: A claim is a statement like “this demo renders a triangle with a render loop,” or “this uses one shader module,” or “this supports resizing.” Proof is whatever lets a stranger confirm the claim without trusting you, usually a link to a specific file, a function, or a demo URL that actually loads. A mismatch is any sentence you cannot prove in under one minute

sourceMaterial.content: Traffic is a vanity metric for local businesses. You can have 5,000 monthly visitors and zero calls. You can have 800 visitors and a full schedule. The difference is not traffic. It is whether you are measuring the actions that actually lead to revenue. This guide covers how to track calls, form submissions, and direction requests so you know whether your local SEO is working. The short answer Stop tracking pageviews as your primary metric. Track three things instead: phone calls, form submissions, and direction requests. Use Google Analytics 4 events for form submissions, Google Business Profile insights for calls and direction requests, and call tracking numbers if you need to know which source drove the call. Review the numbers monthly and compare them to the previous month and the same

sourceMaterial.title: measure calls forms direction requests
sourceMaterial.content: month last year. Why traffic alone is useless A local business website is not a media site. Its job is not to get eyeballs. Its job is to generate leads. If you are ranking 1 for "plumber Rockford" and getting 1,200 clicks a month but your phone is not ringing, something is broken. Maybe your site loads slowly. Maybe your phone number is not visible. Maybe your reviews are bad. Maybe the traffic is coming from the wrong search intent. You will not know any of this if you are only looking at traffic. You need to track the actions that happen after the click. What to track Phone calls Phone calls are the primary conversion for most local service businesses. When someone needs a plumber, they call. They do not fill out a contact form and wait. Track calls from three sources: 1. Your website:

Other directories: Yelp, Bing, and other citations that show your number Form submissions Forms matter for businesses with longer sales cycles or higher ticket services. A homeowner researching a roof replacement might fill out a form instead of calling. Track every form submission as a conversion. Direction requests Direction requests are a strong intent signal. If someone is asking for directions to your business, they are planning to visit. Google Business Profile tracks this for you. GBP actions GBP insights also tracks: Website clicks from your listing Photo views Message interactions Booking clicks (if you use booking features) These are secondary

Log into your GBP dashboard and look at the performance section. You will see calls, direction requests, website clicks, and message interactions over the last 7, 30, or 90 days. Call tracking (optional) If you want to know which source drove a call (organic search vs. Yelp vs. a direct mailer), use a call tracking service. You need to know whether that call came from your website, your Google Business Profile, Yelp, or a paid ad. The cleanest way is call tracking with dynamic number insertion (DNI). CallRail and similar services do this. You place a small JavaScript snippet on your site. When a visitor lands on your site from organic search, the script swaps your real phone number for a tracking number on the page. When they call that tracking number, CallRail forwards it to your real line and logs the source as organic search. But if you are running ads, doing SEO, and listed on multiple directories, DNI is the only way to know which channel is actually driving calls. A simpler approach that works for smaller budgets: use a unique phone number on your website that is not listed anywhere else. Any call to that number came from your site. It is not as precise as DNI (it cannot tell you organic vs. paid), but it tells you website calls vs. everything else. I have set this up for clients using Twilio numbers that cost about $1/month plus per minute usage. It is not free, but it is close. Everything else is secondary. Website clicks, photo views, and search impressions are useful context, but they do not pay the bills. If calls are up and traffic is flat, you are winning. If you are not using GTM, form tracking is harder than it needs to be. Formspark or Netlify Forms — if your site is static, these handle form submissions and can fire GA4 events on success without a backend. I start most clients with GBP forwarding numbers and GA4 form tracking through GTM. That covers 80% of what matters for free. CallRail gets added when the business is spending money on ads or needs to know which directory is

If your call conversion rate is below 1%, the problem is on the website. Check whether your phone number is visible above the fold on mobile without scrolling. Check whether it is a clickable tel: link. Check whether there is a clear call to action within the first screen. sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: Most posts about AI tooling either sound like marketing or sound like someone trying to show off a stack. This is neither. This post is simply a description of the tools I have actually used, what each one is, what it is good at, what it is bad at, and why I choose one over another depending on the situation. There is no “workflow philosophy” here. No productivity system. No grand claims. Just a straightforward breakdown of editors, AI agents, local models, hosted models, and autocomplete tools, and what each of them is useful for in practice. Three buckets: editors, terminals, and models If you blend these together, everything sounds like marketing. Separating them makes it understandable. Editors are where you navigate a repo, search, make changes, review diffs, and keep context. VS Code

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: is the editor I use the most. Cursor and Kiro are also editors, but they are AI first editors. Cline is not really an editor by itself. It is an agent that lives inside VS Code and can operate on the repo. Terminal tools are the stuff that proves whether anything is real. Running builds, running tests, running scripts, looking at logs, and reading errors. AI can help interpret output, but the terminal is still the source of truth because it is the thing that can tell you “this compiles” or “this fails” without opinion. Models are the brains. Local models (like Qwen through Ollama) are fast and cheap, and they are good for constant small tasks. Bigger hosted models (like Claude) are slower and cost more, but they handle wider context and messier reasoning better. Model choice matters

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: because the same tool behaves differently depending on what brain you attach to it. VS Code VS Code is just the editor. It is not an AI product. The reason it stays central for me is boring but real. It is where I can search across a repo, jump between definitions and references, compare diffs, keep multiple terminals open, and not lose my place. If you have ever tried to refactor a project without solid search and navigation, you know why that matters. (VS Code documentation) When AI is involved, VS Code matters even more because it is the place where I can review what the AI changed. Most AI mistakes are not obvious until you look at the diff and notice it changed a pattern, renamed something inconsistently, or introduced a new style in a file that already had a standard. So VS Code is

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: not “the AI tool.” It is the control room. Cline Cline is a VS Code extension that acts like an agent. The important detail is not that it can chat. The important detail is that it can see the repo and operate on it. It can browse the file tree, open files, propose patches in the right places, run commands, then react to the output that comes back. (Cline on GitHub) That repo awareness is the whole reason it is useful. A normal chat model will happily give you a snippet that does not match your project. Cline can look at your actual project structure and aim the changes at real files. Where Cline shines is scoped work that still needs real repo context. Fix a broken import chain. Trace where a route is defined. Update a component but keep the existing patterns. Find why the build fails and

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: propose a patch. It is basically good at “help me move in the repo” tasks. Where Cline gets dangerous is when you let it do large refactors without tight boundaries. Agents can churn code. They can change styles mid stream. They can move files to places that feel neat to them but not to you. The way I keep it safe is treating it like a patch assistant. Small tasks, review diffs, run the app, repeat. Ollama Ollama is a local model runner. That means it is not the model itself, it is the thing that hosts models on your machine. The reason I use it is because it makes AI help feel like a normal tool instead of a separate activity. No tabs, no waiting on a website, no thinking about tokens every time I ask for help. (Ollama website) Local running also changes the vibe in a practical way. You

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: ask more questions because the cost is basically your hardware, not a meter. That matters when you are doing day to day cleanup work and you just want quick answers without turning it into a production. The tradeoff is obvious too. Local models have a ceiling. They can be great for constant small work, but they are not always great when the bug is conceptual or the fix depends on understanding a wide slice of the app. Qwen models When I say Qwen here, I mean the Qwen models I have run locally through Ollama. I like them for the boring, constant, real tasks that every repo has. They are fast enough that you can keep them “on” mentally and just use them like a helper while you work. (Qwen on Hugging Face) The kinds of tasks that fit Qwen well are things like cleaning up a component so it

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: reads like a human wrote it, extracting repeated logic into a helper, fixing TypeScript errors where the intent is obvious, reorganizing imports, writing small utilities, or giving you a first pass implementation that you are going to review and adjust anyway. The kinds of tasks that fit Qwen poorly are the ones where the model needs to hold a wide context, like multi file data flow, tricky auth behavior, subtle WebGPU pipeline issues, or deployment failures where the fix depends on understanding the environment and not just the code. When a local model starts guessing confidently, that is when it becomes slower than just switching to a stronger brain. Claude models Claude is the model I switch to when the problem stops being “small code work” and becomes “reasoning work.” Multi file bugs.

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: Messy code that needs a rewrite without changing behavior. Build errors that have more than one root cause. Situations where you need an explanation that maps back to your files and not just a generic answer. (Claude by Anthropic) The difference is not magic. The difference is that it tends to keep a larger mental model at once, and it is better at explaining why a fix is the fix. That matters because patching the symptom is easy, but patching the cause is what keeps the repo from turning into a haunted house. The downside is cost and overkill. If you use a stronger model for every tiny change, you waste time. You also start accepting changes you did not fully understand because the output looks confident. So for me Claude is a switch, not a default. I use it when the problem deserves it.

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: Cursor Cursor is an AI first editor. The way I think about it is that VS Code is my stable home, and Cursor is the tool I open when the codebase shape is the problem. That does not mean “I need help writing code.” It means the repo is messy enough that doing changes one file at a time is painful, and you need a broader restructuring pass. (Cursor website) Cursor is useful when you want consistent changes across many files. Renaming patterns. Reorganizing folders. Pulling a feature into a cleaner structure. Refactoring repeated patterns in a React codebase. Stuff that would be annoying and error prone if you tried to do it manually across a lot of files. The risk is the same as any wide tool. It can produce a huge diff that is hard to review. If you cannot review it, you cannot trust it. So

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: I only use Cursor when I am willing to do the review work and I have a clear goal for the refactor. Kiro Kiro is another AI first IDE, and for me it only matters when the blocker is AWS output and configuration. IAM failures. S3 policy behavior. CloudWatch logs. CLI errors. Deployments that technically finished but the app does not behave. The reason an AI IDE can help in this category is not that it invents architecture. It is that it can help you interpret error messages, map them to configuration, and propose small changes you can test. AWS debugging is mostly reading and iterating. A tool that can keep track of the context of an error and help you form the next test can save time. The risk is when it starts hallucinating solutions that do not match what AWS is actually returning. If it

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: is not grounded in the exact output you are seeing, it becomes noise. So Kiro is not always open. It is a tool I open when the problem is clearly in AWS land. GitHub Copilot Copilot is autocomplete. That is the honest description. It is good at finishing JSX lines, filling in small helper functions, and saving you from typing boilerplate. It is not good at owning architecture decisions or understanding your whole repo. (GitHub Copilot) If you treat Copilot like a small typing tool, it is helpful. If you treat it like a decision maker, it will push patterns that do not match your codebase and you will spend time cleaning up drift. Why model choice matters depending on the tool This is the part that usually gets skipped. People talk about tools like the tool is the brain. It is not. The

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: model is the brain. Cline is an agent layer. It can talk to a local model through Ollama or it can talk to a hosted model. That choice changes how it behaves. If you attach a local model, you get fast, cheap iteration for small fixes, and you accept that it will hit a ceiling. If you attach a stronger hosted model, you get deeper reasoning, but you also need to keep scope tighter because big brains produce big edits. Cursor and Kiro are similar. They are editors with AI capability, but the model quality and context handling changes what they are good at. The more the task looks like “understand this whole system,” the more model quality matters. The more the task looks like “help me write this small piece cleanly,” the more speed matters. A breakdown that actually separates tools from

sourceMaterial.title: my real ai development setup
sourceMaterial.content: models Before the table, this is the clearest way I know how to say it. Tools are the interface. Models are the reasoning engine. Terminals are the truth. sourceMaterial.content: Mobile prototypes only matter if they run on an actual simulator or device. A repo that “looks right” but will not boot is just text. This post is a small React Native prototype you can verify. The goal is not to build an app. The goal is to create a fresh project, change one file, and prove you can see your change on screen. Once you can do that, everything else becomes normal incremental work instead of guesswork. What you are building You are building the smallest possible React Native app that prints a single line of text in a safe area. That sounds boring, but it is the right baseline because it proves the entire chain works: Node can run the CLI, the native project exists, the bundler can serve JavaScript, the native shell can load it, and the screen can render. React Native is just

sourceMaterial.title: native react
sourceMaterial.content: React code running inside a native shell (Source). The “native” part is real. iOS builds use Xcode (Source). Android builds use Gradle and the Android toolchain (Source). The JavaScript is still yours, but the last mile is a real native app. What you need and why you need it React Native is one of those setups where missing one piece can waste a whole night. So here is what matters and why. You need Node because the React Native CLI is a Node tool (Source). You need Xcode if you plan to run iOS because iOS builds are Xcode projects under the hood (Source). You need Android Studio if you plan to run Android because it provides the SDK, emulator, and build tools that Gradle expects (Source). Here is a quick summary of what each prerequisite gives you: Node.js — runs the React Native CLI and

They are not “optional best practices.” They are just the fastest way to confirm you are not walking into a setup trap. 1. Check Node — confirm Node is installed and not an ancient version (Source) 2. Check Xcode (iOS only) — confirm command line tools are installed and the license is accepted (Source) 3. Check Android Studio (Android only) — confirm the SDK is installed and at least one emulator image exists (Source) First, confirm Node exists and is not ancient. bash node v npm v If you do not see versions printed, stop and fix Node first. If you do not have an emulator that can boot, run android has nothing to target. How to build it Step 1: Create the project This is the scaffold step. It creates the repo, the native shells, and the default starter app. bash npx react native@latest init NativeLab cd NativeLab What that command actually does matters. It generates a project folder, installs the JavaScript dependencies, and creates the native folders ( ios/ and android/ ) that Xcode and Gradle will build (Source). If those folders do not exist, you do not have a

If it fails, do not try to “fix it by guessing.” Read the exact CLI output. Most failures are missing prerequisites or permissions. Step 2: Edit the one file that proves everything React Native projects can get noisy fast. The point here is to keep the first change dead simple so you can see the feedback loop. Open App.tsx and replace it with this: tsx export default function App() Here is what that code is doing in plain terms.
