If you have Google reviews from customers in Belvidere, reference them. This is the strongest signal that the page is real. 6. Service area map. A real map showing your coverage area, not a stock image. 7. Internal links. Link to your main service pages and to adjacent city pages. Do not link only to your homepage. The test is simple: if you removed the city name from the page, would the remaining content still be unique and useful? If yes, you have a real page. If the page collapses into generic boilerplate, it is a doorway page and you should rewrite it. A real service area business SEO strategy Here is the actual strategy I used for a client

Six pages, one per city. Each had a unique intro written from the owner's experience working in that city. The Belvidere page mentioned a specific neighborhood near I 90 where they had done a furnace replacement that winter. The Loves Park page mentioned a condo complex where they service multiple units. Real details, not templates. Step 3: Citations. NAP standardized across Google, Bing, Apple Maps, Yelp, and Facebook. Same format everywhere. Took one

sourceMaterial.title: service area business seo no storefront

The two they were not ranking in were the most competitive (Rockford itself) and the farthest (Roscoe). By month six, they were in the pack for five of six. The strategy was not clever or complicated. It was consistent execution of the basics. Common mistakes service area businesses make Beyond the fake address problem, there are three mistakes I see repeatedly. Listing cities you do not serve. You add Chicago to your service area because you want the traffic. You get one lead, drive two hours, and lose money on

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: How a single cached file made my entire GitHub Pages site refuse to update, why it happened, and exactly how to fix it if it ever happens to you. Service workers are a browser API designed for offline first web apps (MDN: Service Worker API), but when left unmanaged they can serve stale content indefinitely. What actually happened My GitHub Pages frontend absolutely refused to update after a full rebuild. I deleted the old code, pushed a new Next.js build, cleaned every folder, checked the deploy logs, and refreshed the live site a hundred times. The same old UI kept loading. Same filters button. Same old DOM. It looked like my deploy did not even run. GitHub Pages serves static content directly from a repository branch (GitHub Pages documentation), so a clean deploy should mean a clean

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: site. GitHub Actions passed every time. The artifact had the correct static export. My repo was clean. My build folder was clean. I even ran grep across the entire project looking for any leftover UI code and found nothing. GitHub Actions workflows run in isolated runners and produce artifacts you can inspect (GitHub Actions documentation), so I could confirm the build output was correct. Then I hit the live URL with curl and it returned the correct new markup. But the browser still showed the old one. So at that point the server and the browser disagreed. When that happens, something in the middle is lying to you. And that something was a service worker I did not even know existed. What the actual root problem was A stale service worker was still registered in the browser from an earlier

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: version of the site. I did not write the service worker myself. AI generated it once, and I never questioned it. I did not know what "sw.js" even meant at the time. A service worker sits between the browser and the network. It can intercept requests and decide what to return (MDN: Using Service Workers). My service worker had cached the old version of the site and never let go of it. So even though the server was sending the new version, the browser ignored it. Service workers have a lifecycle with distinct phases — registration, installation, activation, and termination (MDN: Service Worker Lifecycle). The key problem is that an activated service worker persists across browser sessions and continues intercepting requests even after you navigate away and come back. Unless you explicitly

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: unregister it or the service worker code itself calls self.skipWaiting() combined with a cache busting strategy, the old cached content wins every time. The browser trusted the service worker more than the server. This is the exact kind of bug that does not feel logical until you understand how aggressive service worker caching is. The fix that finally worked Here is the fix that instantly solved it: 1. Open your site in Chrome. 2. Open DevTools with Ctrl + Shift + I or Cmd + Option + I (Chrome DevTools documentation). 3. Go to the Application tab. 4. Click Service Workers on the left. 5. You will see one or more registered service workers. Look for anything like sw.js or service worker.js , or anything showing “activated.” 6. Click Unregister . 7. Refresh the page. If the service worker

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: was the problem, the new version of the site will load instantly. No delay. No waiting. It is one of the most dramatic “instant fix” moments you can have in web development. Comparison of debugging methods When your site refuses to update, there are three fast ways to narrow down the cause. Here is how they compare: Method What it checks Speed What a positive result means curl the live URL Server side HTML output Seconds If curl shows new HTML but the browser does not, the problem is client side caching Open in Incognito Fresh browser session with no service workers Seconds If Incognito shows the new version, a service worker or cache is the culprit DevTools Application tab Registered service workers and cache storage Seconds Directly confirms whether a stale service worker is registered

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: and active This is the exact moment it hit me that the entire issue was not my code or GitHub Pages. It was a cached worker from a build that did not exist anymore. How to confirm this is your issue too Here are the fastest ways to check if you have the same problem. 1. Hit your site with curl Run this in your terminal: bash curl sL https://your site.github.io head curl fetches the raw HTML from the server without any browser caching or service worker interference (curl documentation). If the HTML here is newer than what your browser is showing, your browser is being lied to. 2. Open your site in Incognito If Incognito shows the new version but your normal browser does not, that is almost always a service worker or cache problem. 3. Check DevTools Look for an active service worker. If you

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: see one and you did not explicitly write it, that is probably the issue. Why this problem happens to many developers Service workers are extremely powerful. They allow offline support, caching, background syncing, and more (MDN: Service Worker API). But the downside is that they aggressively hold onto cached files. This is on purpose. They are designed to keep apps working even if the network dies. The problem is that GitHub Pages does not know anything about your service worker. So even after a fresh deploy, the browser can still keep serving old files because the worker is literally intercepting every request. GitHub Pages is a static hosting service (GitHub Pages documentation) and has no way to invalidate browser side service worker caches. This is why so many people complain that

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: their GitHub Pages site does not update after a deploy. The deploy is fine. The browser is not. Why this deserves a blog post Because it is one of the most confusing and frustrating bugs you can hit as a newer developer. You can spend hours thinking your deploy is wrong, your build is wrong, your repo is wrong, or GitHub Pages is broken. But the truth is that your browser is simply loading an old cached version from a script you forgot about, or did not know existed. Service workers can hold a website hostage if you are not careful. What I would do differently now Since hitting this issue, here is what I changed in my workflow: I never generate a service worker unless I know why I need it. Service workers should be added deliberately, not auto generated (MDN: Service Worker Lifecycle). I

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: always check DevTools when a deploy looks stuck. I test live sites in Incognito to avoid cache issues. I keep build processes simple until I fully understand what is happening. I clean out all AI generated files before deploying anything. I add a cache busting version query string (e.g. ?v=2 ) to script tags when testing updates. I verify deploys with curl before trusting the browser view. Caching bugs like this are sneaky and they waste time, but once you see how they work, they are easy to avoid. Final takeaway If your website refuses to update even though your deploy is clean, it might be a stale service worker. You can confirm this by comparing the server output with curl and checking the Application tab in DevTools. Unregistering the worker fixes the issue instantly. This bug taught

sourceMaterial.title: service worker held site hostage
sourceMaterial.content: me more about how the browser actually works than almost anything else I have built so far. sourceMaterial.title: small business website checklist illinois
sourceMaterial.content: Most small business websites I look at are not broken because they lack a fancy feature. They are broken because a visitor cannot figure out three basic things: what the business does, who it helps, and how to contact it. Research backs this up: Google's research on mobile user experience found that users form judgments about a company's credibility in as little as 50 milliseconds, and 57% of users say they will not recommend a business with a poorly designed mobile site (Google mobile experience research). I made this checklist for a concrete siding company in Durand a while back. It applies to almost any local service business in Northwest Illinois. What should a small business website include? A small business website should answer three questions within seconds: what the business does,

sourceMaterial.title: small business website checklist illinois
sourceMaterial.content: who it helps, and what the next step is. It needs a clear service area, one obvious contact method, mobile friendly layout, one job per page, real photos instead of broad claims, and clean technical basics like page titles and meta descriptions. Clarity beats fancy features every time. The essential elements every small business website needs: Clear value proposition — what you do, stated in plain language above the fold Defined service area — the towns, counties, or regions you actually serve One obvious contact method — a phone number, email, or form that is easy to find Mobile friendly layout — readable text, tappable buttons, no horizontal scrolling (Google mobile friendly test criteria) One job per page — each page focuses on a single service or topic Real photos — actual photos of

Start by fixing mobile layout, since most local traffic comes from phones — over 60% of web traffic is mobile (Statista mobile traffic share). Make sure text is not cramped and buttons are easy to tap. State your service area plainly so visitors know you are local. Give every page one job so it does not feel cluttered. Use real photos and honest service descriptions instead of inflated copy. Make contact obvious with one form or email. Steps to improve a local business website for customers: 1. Audit mobile layout first — open the site on a phone and try

sourceMaterial.title: small business website checklist illinois

Replace stock photos with real ones — show actual work, vehicles, team members, or location 6. Write honest service descriptions — describe what you actually do, not what sounds impressive 7. Make contact obvious — one form or email, visible in the header or footer of every page Why is my small business website not getting leads? sourceMaterial.title: small business website checklist illinois

Fix clarity first: better structure, plain service area language, and one obvious call to action. Common reasons small business websites lose leads: Unclear service offering — the homepage says "quality you can trust" but never says what the business actually does Hidden contact information — the phone number or form is buried at the bottom of the page or on a separate tab No service area stated — visitors cannot tell if the business serves their town Slow mobile experience — pages take too long to load or are hard to read on a phone (Google PageSpeed Insights) No call to action — the visitor reaches the end of a page and does

If the first screen is all slogans and no service description, the visitor has to work too hard. Most will not. 2. Say where you work plainly If you serve Durand, Davis, or nearby Illinois communities, say it directly. Do not make people guess whether you are local, remote, or in another state. This is not about stuffing town names into every sentence. It is about giving the human visitor and the search engine one clean signal. 3. Make contact obvious One main email or form. One clear call to action. A short note about what

Mobile cleanup is usually the highest value fix on an older site. sourceMaterial.content: on a VPS or AWS Lambda Netlify functions are great for short tasks, not long workers Quick database prototype Supabase or a JSON file Fastest path to persisted state in a demo Native mobile experiment React Native I am not great at it yet, but it is the fastest way to get a real app on a phone The pattern is simple: I start with the default stack, then switch only when the project genuinely needs something else. Not when I am bored. Tools I tried but did not keep I have used a lot of frameworks over the last few years. Here is where some of them landed: Prisma: Great DX, but I usually do not need an ORM on small projects. Raw SQL or a thin query layer is enough. shadcn/ui: Good components. I use it as inspiration more than a dependency because I want to own my CSS tokens. Bun: Fast. I use

sourceMaterial.title: technical stack
sourceMaterial.content: it for scripts, but I still deploy Node because hosting compatibility matters more than local speed. Redux/Zustand: Rarely needed now. Server state or URL state usually covers what I used to put in global stores. This list is not criticism. These tools are good. They are just not my defaults. How this stack has evolved This is not the stack I started with. Three years ago, this site was plain HTML and CSS with no framework. Two years ago, it was Gatsby with JavaScript and styled components. The current version is Gatsby with TypeScript, Theme UI, and Tailwind. The evolution was driven by real problems, not novelty. I moved from JavaScript to TypeScript after spending two days debugging a shape error that TypeScript would have caught at compile time. I added Tailwind after realizing I was

sourceMaterial.title: technical stack
sourceMaterial.content: writing the same utility classes over and over in custom CSS. I kept Theme UI because ripping it out would mean rewriting every page's styling, and the benefit did not justify the risk. The one change I regret is not adopting TypeScript sooner. I resisted it because it felt like overhead on small projects. In practice, it saves me more time on small projects than on large ones, because small projects have less test coverage and fewer eyes on the code. Trade offs of the current stack Every stack has costs. Here are the real ones I live with. Build speed. Gatsby builds this site in about 90 seconds locally. For a site with 50+ pages and a heavy image pipeline, that is acceptable but not fast. Next.js with the App Router builds comparable sites in 30 40 seconds. I accept the slower build

sourceMaterial.title: technical stack
sourceMaterial.content: because the GraphQL data layer and image pipeline save me more time during development than I lose during builds. Bundle size. The inlined CSS is about 194KB. That is larger than I would like, but it is a known Gatsby behavior and the site scores well on Core Web Vitals regardless. If bundle size became a real problem, I would externalize the CSS, but I am not willing to re test every theme to save 100KB that does not affect the metrics that matter. Developer experience. TypeScript adds friction for quick edits. Tailwind's class lists get long and hard to read. Theme UI's sx prop causes a persistent type error in the layout component that I have chosen not to fix because it is a theme ui typing issue, not a real bug. These are tolerable annoyances, not dealbreakers. Hosting lock in.

sourceMaterial.title: technical stack
sourceMaterial.content: Netlify's functions, identity widget, and redirect system are convenient, but they create mild lock in. Moving to Vercel or a VPS would require reworking serverless functions and auth. I accept this because the convenience outweighs the migration cost for the projects I actually ship. What I would choose if starting fresh today If I were building this site from scratch tomorrow, the stack would be different in a few specific ways. Astro instead of Gatsby. Astro builds faster, has a smaller output, and supports MDX natively. Gatsby's GraphQL layer is powerful but unnecessary for a content site. Astro's content collections give me the type safety I need without the build overhead. TypeScript from day one. No question. The type safety is worth the setup cost. Tailwind, same as now. Nothing

sourceMaterial.title: technical stack

The specific tools would shift, but the philosophy is the same. Start simple, add complexity only when a real problem demands it. I have abandoned perfectly good stacks because a new release got attention, then regretted it two weeks later. The rule I

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: I have abandoned more test suites than I care to admit. I would start with a vow to write 100% coverage, add a Cypress suite, then spend weeks debugging flaky tests because a div moved two pixels. Eventually I stopped running npm test altogether. The problem was not a lack of desire. It was the strategy. I was building an ice cream cone: a few unit tests at the bottom and a massive layer of slow UI tests on top. That is exhausting. Now I use a much smaller stack: fast unit tests for pure logic, and a short manual smoke protocol for the rest. Why do my test suites keep failing or getting abandoned? Most test suites get abandoned because they become a maintenance burden instead of a safety net. The common pattern is building an ice cream cone: a few unit tests at the bottom and a massive

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: layer of slow, flaky UI tests on top. When tests break because a div moved two pixels, you eventually stop running them. The fix is a smaller, faster stack. What is the best testing strategy for small and solo projects? For solo and small projects, the best strategy is a small testing pyramid: fast unit tests with Vitest for pure logic like data transformations and formatters, plus a short manual smoke checklist for the rest. Skip E2E frameworks like Cypress and Playwright unless you have a team to maintain them. Automate the unit tests in CI and keep the smoke check manual. How do I set up Vitest for unit testing in a Vite project? Vitest is the easiest unit test runner for Vite projects because it reads your existing Vite config and supports ESM and TypeScript out of the box. Install it

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: with npm install D vitest, add test scripts to your package.json, and write focused tests on pure logic. Tests run in milliseconds and catch null values, bad date parsing, and wrong booleans. Level 1: unit tests with vitest For a while I used Jest, but ESM and TypeScript kept creating configuration friction. Vitest reads my existing Vite config, supports ESM out of the box, and runs fast. Setup is minimal: bash npm install D vitest @vitest/coverage v8 json } I keep tests focused on pure logic: data transformations, formatters, anything where the same input should always produce the same output. For example: typescript describe('formatUser utility', () = as const; expect(formatUser(input).fullName).toBe('Guest'); }); it('identifies admin privileges', () = as const;

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: expect(formatUser(input).isAdmin).toBe(true); }); }); These run in milliseconds. They catch the boring mistakes: null values, bad date parsing, wrong booleans. That is the highest return I get from testing. Here are three real bugs that unit tests caught before they shipped: 1. A formatDate function that parsed ISO strings with new Date(input) worked for valid dates but returned "Invalid Date" for empty strings instead of falling back to a default. The test fed it "" and the assertion failed loudly. 2. A price formatter that was supposed to round to two decimals used Math.round instead of toFixed(2) , so $19.995 became 20 instead of "20.00" . The test caught the type mismatch — the function returned a number when the contract said string. 3. A role check helper returned true for the string

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: "admin" but also for "administrator" because it used startsWith("admin") . The test asserted that only exact "admin" should pass, and it failed. None of those are glamorous. But each one would have surfaced in production as a visible bug, and each took under five minutes to write a test for. Level 2: the manual smoke protocol I do not run E2E tests on personal projects. Cypress and Playwright are powerful, but maintaining them for a solo project is often more work than the bugs they catch. That said, I do use a small number of integration tests for the boundaries between modules — not full E2E, but tests that exercise two or three functions together. For example, a test that calls a fetchUser function (which hits a mocked fetch) and pipes the result through formatUser catches wiring bugs

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: that a pure unit test on formatUser alone would miss. I keep these in Vitest alongside the unit tests using vi.mock() to stub the network layer. Here is the breakdown of test types I actually use: Unit tests (Vitest) — pure functions, formatters, parsers, role checks. Same input, same output. These are 90% of my test files. Integration tests (Vitest with mocks) — two or three modules wired together, network stubbed. Maybe 10% of files. Example: fetchUser + formatUser + a cache layer. E2E (manual smoke check) — the checklist below. No Playwright, no Cypress. I am the runner. The one time I did add a Playwright suite for a client project, it caught a real production issue: a form submission flow that worked in Chrome but failed in Firefox because of a submit event ordering difference. That

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: was worth the maintenance cost on a team. On a solo project, I would have caught the same thing in the manual smoke check the first time I tested in Firefox. Instead I keep a short checklist in docs/QA SMOKE CHECK.md and walk through it before a release: markdown Release smoke check Home page loads with no console errors. Primary user flow works end to end. Mobile menu opens and closes. Footer links do not 404. Manual checks force me to look at the app. I notice layout shifts, slow interactions, and broken links that automated assertions would miss. Level 3: CI for the unit tests only I automate the fast part. The smoke check stays manual. My GitHub Actions workflow looks like this: yaml name: Unit Tests on: push: branches: [main] pull request: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs on: ubuntu

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: latest steps: uses: actions/checkout@v4 uses: actions/setup node@v4 with: node version: 20 cache: 'npm' run: npm ci run: npm test Nothing fancy. It just makes sure the unit tests run somewhere other than my laptop. How testing fits into my workflow The workflow is simple and I do not over engineer it: 1. Write the function. Get it working in the REPL or a scratch file. 2. Write one or two unit tests for the edge cases I already thought about while writing it — null inputs, empty strings, boundary values. 3. Run npm test locally. If it passes, commit. 4. Push. CI runs the same vitest run command. If it fails, I get a red X on the commit and fix it before merging. 5. Before a release , walk the smoke checklist manually in Chrome and Firefox. I do not write tests first. I do not aim for a

sourceMaterial.title: testing matters
sourceMaterial.content: coverage number. I write tests for the functions where a bug would be embarrassing or hard to trace — formatters, parsers, permission checks, anything with money or dates in it. Everything else gets the smoke check. What I deliberately skip I am honest about the gaps. No visual regression testing. No full integration tests. Mostly Chrome based checks. Those are real risks, but for personal projects the maintenance cost is not worth it. I would rather ship and verify by hand than maintain a brittle E2E suite I stop running. Closing Testing is not binary. It is a confidence trade off. I use fast unit tests for logic that must be right and a short smoke protocol for everything else. That gives me most of the confidence with a fraction of the maintenance.

sourceMaterial.title: webgpu getting started
sourceMaterial.content: The first WebGPU triangle is the hardest one. Not because the API is complicated, but because the pipeline has so many small gates. Adapter, device, canvas context, format, shader entry points, render pass, draw call — if any one of them is off, you get a blank canvas and no useful error. This guide is the guide I wish I had when I started. It covers the minimal setup, the common failures, and a verification step after every stage so you know exactly where things break. I cannot run these steps from this blog repo, so treat it as a lab guide. Open a local folder, follow each step, and check the outcome before moving on. What you will build By the end you will have: A canvas bound to WebGPU A requested adapter and device A minimal render pipeline One blue triangle on a dark background A

sourceMaterial.title: webgpu getting started
sourceMaterial.content: loop that keeps it rendering One honest triangle is worth more than a thousand copied demos. WebGPU in five words At its core, WebGPU is: Adapter: the GPU capability entry point. Device: the object that creates GPU resources. Pipeline: the configuration that ties shaders to output. Context: the bridge between WebGPU and the canvas. Render pass: the command that actually draws. If those five pieces line up, you get a triangle. If one is missing or mismatched, you get silence. What you need Chrome 113+, Edge, or any browser with stable WebGPU support A local static server (I use npx serve or VS Code Live Server) I recommend a local server because module scripts and WebGPU can behave differently when opened as a raw file:// URL. Browser support matrix WebGPU shipped stable in Chrome 113 (May

sourceMaterial.title: webgpu getting started
sourceMaterial.content: 2023). Here is where things stand as of writing: Browser Support Notes Chrome / Edge 113+ Stable, enabled by default Safari 17+ (macOS 14, iOS 17) Stable as of Safari 17.4 Firefox Nightly only Behind dom.webgpu.enabled flag in Nightly. Not in stable release builds yet. Mobile Chrome (Android) 121+ Stable on supported devices If navigator.gpu is undefined, your browser either does not support WebGPU or it is behind a flag. On Linux, you may need to launch Chrome with enable features=Vulkan if hardware acceleration is not detected automatically. On older hardware without a compatible GPU driver, requestAdapter() returns null and there is no workaround. Step 1: Create the HTML shell Create index.html with a canvas and a module script: html Open it in the browser. You should see a blank page

sourceMaterial.title: webgpu getting started
sourceMaterial.content: and no console errors. If you see a 404 for main.js , the script path is wrong. Fix that before continuing. A blank canvas at this stage is success. It means the browser is ready for WebGPU, and we have not introduced any API code yet. Step 2: Request the adapter and device Create main.js and add the first WebGPU calls: js const adapter = await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter(); if (!adapter) throw new Error("No GPU adapter"); const device = await adapter.requestDevice(); This is the first real gate. requestAdapter asks the browser for a GPU. If it returns null , WebGPU is not enabled or not available. requestDevice gives you the object every later call depends on. You can pass options to requestAdapter to request a specific power preference: js const adapter = await

sourceMaterial.title: webgpu getting started
sourceMaterial.content: navigator.gpu.requestAdapter( ); Use "high performance" on laptops with dual GPUs to force the discrete card. Use "low power" for battery sensitive contexts. If you omit it, the browser picks a default, which is usually the integrated GPU on laptops, and that can be slower than you expect. Open DevTools. No thrown error means you passed. If you get No GPU adapter , check that your browser supports WebGPU and that any required flags are enabled. On some systems the integrated GPU is enough. Step 3: Configure the canvas context Now bind the canvas to WebGPU: js const canvas = document.getElementById("gfx"); const context = canvas.getContext("webgpu"); const format = navigator.gpu.getPreferredCanvasFormat(); context.configure( ); The format returned by getPreferredCanvasFormat must match the

sourceMaterial.title: webgpu getting started
sourceMaterial.content: format your pipeline targets later. Mismatched formats are one of the most common reasons for a blank screen. I use alphaMode: "opaque" because transparency is rarely needed for a first demo and can introduce subtle bugs. No console errors here means the canvas is ready to receive frames. If context is null , double check the canvas ID and make sure the browser really supports WebGPU — not all canvas contexts do. Step 4: Build a minimal pipeline The pipeline connects your WGSL shader to the render pass. Start with the smallest shader possible: js const shaderCode = @vertex fn vs main(@builtin(vertex index) vi: u32) @builtin(position) vec4f @fragment fn fs main() @location(0) vec4f ; Then create the pipeline: js const module = device.createShaderModule( ); const pipeline =

sourceMaterial.title: webgpu getting started
sourceMaterial.content: device.createRenderPipeline( , fragment: ] }, primitive: }); I keep the shader self contained because it removes one variable from debugging. If the triangle does not appear later, I know the problem is not a missing shader file or import path. No shader compile errors in the console means the syntax is valid and the entry points were found. Step 5: Draw the frame The render pass is where everything finally connects: js function frame() , loadOp: "clear", storeOp: "store" }] }); pass.setPipeline(pipeline); pass.draw(3); pass.end(); device.queue.submit([encoder.finish()]); requestAnimationFrame(frame); } frame(); loadOp: "clear" is important. Without it, the triangle can flicker or leave leftover pixels from previous frames. requestAnimationFrame keeps the loop running. At this point you

sourceMaterial.title: webgpu getting started
sourceMaterial.content: should see a blue triangle on a dark background. If you do, the entire pipeline is healthy. Verify it worked Check these three things: 1. The triangle is visible. 2. The console has no errors. 3. The frame keeps rendering without flicker. If all three are true, you have a solid baseline. Every later feature — uniforms, buffers, resize handling — builds on top of this. Common mistakes Symptom Likely cause Fix navigator.gpu is undefined WebGPU disabled or unsupported Enable flags or update the browser Blank canvas Format mismatch between context and pipeline Use the same format variable everywhere Flickering triangle Missing or wrong loadOp Set loadOp: "clear" Shader compile error Wrong entry point name or WGSL syntax Copy the exact names from the shader Quick cheat sheet 1. Request adapter

Next steps Once the triangle is stable, the smallest useful upgrades are: Resize handling: reconfigure the canvas when the window resizes. A uniform buffer: animate the background color or triangle position. A vertex buffer: move the triangle geometry out of the shader. Pick one, add it, verify it, then pick the next. WebGPU makes more sense when each layer is solid. sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics
sourceMaterial.content: Website accessibility is not a nice to have. It is a legal requirement, a business obligation, and a practical way to make sure every visitor can use your site. For small businesses, the risk is not theoretical. ADA lawsuits over inaccessible websites are filed every day, and they target small companies as often as large ones. The short answer WCAG 2.2 AA is the standard most accessibility laws point to. It means your site works with a keyboard, has text alternatives for images, uses sufficient color contrast, labels every form field, and lets users skip to main content. The most common failures are missing alt text, low contrast, no keyboard navigation, unlabeled forms, and no skip link. You can catch most of these with three free tests: keyboard only navigation, a screen reader pass, and

sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics
sourceMaterial.content: a contrast checker. What WCAG 2.2 AA means WCAG stands for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Version 2.2 is the current standard, published in October 2023. The "AA" level is the middle tier and the one most laws reference, including the ADA and Section 508. WCAG is organized around four principles. Content must be: Perceivable: Users can see or hear it. Images need alt text, videos need captions, content needs sufficient contrast. Operable: Users can navigate it. Keyboard access, no keyboard traps, enough time to read content. Understandable: Users can comprehend it. Clear language, predictable navigation, error prevention on forms. Robust: It works with assistive technology. Proper HTML, ARIA where needed, compatible with screen readers. You do not need to memorize all 86 success

sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics
sourceMaterial.content: criteria. You need to fix the ones that fail most often. The criteria that matter most for small businesses If you focus on the handful of criteria that fail most often on small business sites, you cover the majority of real world risk: 1.1.1 Non text Content — every image has alt text (or empty alt if decorative). This is the single most cited failure in ADA lawsuits. 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) — text meets 4.5:1 contrast against its background. Light gray on white is the usual offender. 1.4.11 Non text Contrast — form borders, focus indicators, and icons need 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors. Most sites miss this one entirely. 2.1.1 Keyboard — every interactive element works with a keyboard. No mouse required. 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap — focus can move in and out of any component without

sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics
sourceMaterial.content: getting stuck. 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks — a skip link or landmark lets keyboard users jump past repeated navigation. 2.4.7 Focus Visible — the focused element has a visible focus indicator. Removing outline without a replacement is a failure. 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions — every form field has a programmatic label, not just a placeholder. 4.1.3 Status Messages — success and error messages are announced to assistive technology without moving focus. These nine criteria are where most small business sites break. Fix them first and you have addressed the bulk of what plaintiffs' attorneys scan for. The most common accessibility failures 1. Missing alt text Every image that conveys information needs an alt attribute that describes what the image shows. Decorative images should have empty alt text (

sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics
sourceMaterial.content: alt="" ) so screen readers skip them. The failure: images with no alt attribute at all, or alt text that says "image" or "photo" or the filename. That tells a screen reader user nothing. The fix: write alt text that describes the content and function of the image. "Team meeting at Durand office" is good alt text. "IMG 4821.jpg" is not. 2. Low color contrast Text needs enough contrast against its background to be readable. WCAG 2.2 AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt or 14pt bold). The failure: light gray text on a white background, or colored text that looks fine to someone with full color vision but is invisible to someone with color blindness. The fix: use a contrast checker (WebAIM's is free and browser based). Test every text and

sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics
sourceMaterial.content: background combination. If the ratio is below 4.5:1, darken the text or lighten the background. 3. No keyboard navigation Not everyone uses a mouse. Some users navigate with a keyboard alone (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space). Every interactive element (links, buttons, form fields) must be reachable and operable with a keyboard. The failure: custom JavaScript widgets that trap focus, links that only work on click, dropdown menus that do not open with keyboard, and no visible focus indicator (the outline that shows which element is selected). The fix: tab through your site without touching the mouse. If you get stuck, that is a keyboard trap. If you cannot tell which element is focused, the focus indicator is missing or removed. 4. Unlabeled form fields Every form input needs a label. Not a

sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics
sourceMaterial.content: placeholder. A placeholder disappears the moment you start typing, and screen readers often do not announce placeholders at all. The failure: forms that use placeholders instead of labels, or labels that are not programmatically connected to their inputs. The fix: use a element with a for attribute that matches the input's id . Every field should have a visible, persistent label. 5. Missing skip link A skip link is a hidden link at the top of the page that lets keyboard users jump directly to the main content. Without it, a keyboard user has to tab through your entire header and navigation on every page. The failure: no skip link, or a skip link that is not visible when focused. The fix: add a "Skip to main content" link as the first element in the body. It should be visually hidden until

sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics

It looks fine to the designer, but it is unreadable for anyone with low vision or in bright ambient light, and it is one of the first things an automated scanner flags. After: html Contact Us 4a4a4a on white is roughly 9.2:1. It passes AAA. The change is a single hex value, it still looks clean, and it resolves a criteria failure that shows up in every audit tool. sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics
sourceMaterial.content: risk ADA Title III applies to websites. Courts have ruled repeatedly that websites are places of public accommodation. You do not need to be a Fortune 500 company to get sued. Plaintiffs' firms file hundreds of these lawsuits per year, many against small businesses, restaurants, and local services. A typical ADA web accessibility lawsuit costs between $5,000 and $25,000 to settle, plus your own legal fees. The cost of fixing the accessibility issues is almost always lower than the cost of a single settlement. sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics

When you fix accessibility issues, you usually improve your search rankings at the same time. Semantic HTML helps both. Using , , , and instead of generic tags gives screen readers and crawlers the same context. A is invisible to a screen reader and ambiguous to Google. Heading structure matters. A single followed by and in order helps screen reader users navigate and helps Google understand your content hierarchy. Skipped levels or multiple tags confuse both. Alt

sourceMaterial.title: website accessibility basics

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: When you hire someone to build your website, you own four things: the domain name, the hosting account, the content (text and images), and the source code. If any of those are in someone else's account or name, you do not fully own your website. Vendor lock in happens when a developer controls one or more of these layers and you cannot leave without starting over. This is the most common problem I see with small business owners. They paid someone to build a site, that person disappeared, and now the business owner cannot update their site, cannot access their domain, and cannot move to a new developer without rebuilding everything. This post explains how to avoid that. For the specifics of how I handle ownership, see my terms and service scope. The four layers of ownership Layer 1: The

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: domain name Your domain name (yourbusiness.com) is the most important asset. If you do not control your domain, you do not control your web presence. Someone can take your entire site offline by pointing the domain elsewhere. What you should own: The domain should be registered in an account with your name and your email on it. You should have the login credentials. You should be the registrant, not the administrative contact on someone else's account. Red flag: Your developer registered the domain "for you" and it is in their GoDaddy or Namecheap account. If they stop responding, you have to file a domain transfer dispute with the registrar, which can take weeks. How I handle it: I help you register the domain in your own account. I walk you through it if you have not done it before. The

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: domain is yours from day one. I am listed as a technical contact if you want, but you are the registrant. Layer 2: The hosting account Hosting is where your website files live. The hosting account controls where the domain points and who can deploy changes to the site. What you should own: The hosting account should be in your name with your payment method. You should have admin access. Your developer can have a collaborator or team member account, but you should be the account owner. Red flag: Your site is hosted on your developer's personal server or their agency's hosting plan, and you have no access. If they go out of business, your site goes down with no warning. How I handle it: For Gatsby sites, I deploy to Netlify. The account is in your name. I am added as a collaborator so I can

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: deploy updates, but you can remove my access anytime. The billing goes to your card. If you stop working with me, you keep the account, the site, and the deploy history. Layer 3: The content Content is the text, images, videos, and any other media on your site. This is what your customers see and what search engines index. What you should own: All content should belong to you. You should have copies of the original text files, the original image files, and the rights to use any stock photography. If you wrote the copy, you own it. If your developer wrote the copy, the contract should specify that the copyright transfers to you on payment. Red flag: Your developer used stock images but did not give you the license information. Or they wrote your copy but the contract says they retain

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: copyright. Or the content only exists inside the CMS and you have no offline copies. How I handle it: You provide the content or I write it as a separate service. Either way, you own it. I send you the source files. For images, I use free licensed stock or images you provide. If paid stock is used, I give you the license receipt. Everything is documented in the service scope. Layer 4: The source code The source code is the actual code that builds your website. For a Gatsby site, this is the React components, the MDX content files, the configuration, and the build scripts. What you should own: You should have access to the full source code, not just the deployed output. This means a Git repository you can clone or download. If your developer built a custom theme or used a proprietary

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: framework, you need to understand what you can and cannot do with it. Red flag: Your developer will not give you the source code. They say "the site is hosted on our platform" and there is no way to export it. This is the most aggressive form of vendor lock in. You are renting your website, not owning it. How I handle it: The source code lives in a Git repository. When the project is done, I transfer the repository to your GitHub account or give you a full archive. The code is yours. If you hire a different developer later, they can clone the repo and take over. I use open source frameworks (Gatsby, React) so any competent developer can work with the codebase. Questions to ask before hiring anyone Before you sign a contract or pay a deposit, ask these questions: 1. Will the domain be

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: registered in my name? Get it in writing. 2. Will the hosting account be in my name? If not, what is the process to transfer it to you? 3. Do I own the content, including copy you write for me? Check the contract for copyright transfer language. 4. Will I receive the source code? In what format? When? 5. What happens if I want to switch developers? Is there a fee? A lock in period? 6. What CMS or platform is the site built on? If it is a proprietary system, you cannot take it with you. 7. Can I export my content? If the answer is no, do not hire them. If a developer dodges these questions or gets defensive, that is your answer. Move on. How vendor lock in actually happens Vendor lock in is rarely malicious. It is usually lazy. A developer registers the domain because it is faster than

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: walking the client through it. They host the site on their own server because it is cheaper. They do not hand over the source code because it is easier to keep it in their own repo. But the result for you is the same. When that developer stops responding, you are stuck. I have talked to business owners who lost their domain because a developer let it expire. I have talked to people who had to rebuild their entire site because the developer's hosting shut down and there was no backup. The fix is simple: own your accounts from the start. It takes 20 minutes to register a domain and set up a hosting account. A developer who will not let you do that is not worth hiring. How to verify you own your website If you are not sure whether you actually own your website, here is how to check each layer

sourceMaterial.content: in under 10 minutes. Domain Go to your domain registrar (GoDaddy, Namecheap, Google Domains, Cloudflare). Log in with your email. Do you see your domain listed? Is your name on the registrant contact? If you cannot log in, or the domain is not in your account, you do not own it. Call the registrar and ask who the registrant is. If it is your developer, you need to initiate a transfer. Hosting Log into your hosting account (Netlify, Vercel, Bluehost, SiteGround). Is the account in your name with your payment method? Can you see your site listed? If your developer logs in with their own credentials and you have no access, you do not own the hosting. Source code Ask your developer for the Git repository. Content Do you have the original text files and images somewhere outside the website? If the only copy of your content lives inside a CMS you cannot access, you do not fully own your content. Export it now. What happens when you do not own your website I have seen this play out three times in the last year. A restaurant in northern Illinois had their site built by a freelancer who registered the domain in his own name. He stopped responding to emails. The domain expired. The site went down. The restaurant had to file a domain recovery dispute with the registrar, which took six weeks. During that time, their Google Business

sourceMaterial.title: website ownership domain hosting content
sourceMaterial.content: Profile pointed to a dead site. A landscaping company had their site hosted on their developer's personal server. The developer got a full time job and shut down the server. No warning. No backup. The company lost three years of content and had to rebuild from scratch. A consulting firm had a custom CMS built by an agency. When they wanted to switch developers, they discovered the CMS was proprietary. No other developer could work with it. They had to rebuild the entire site on a standard platform. In every case, the fix was the same: own your accounts from the start. The recovery is always harder and more expensive than the prevention. How to transfer ownership if your developer holds the keys If you are already locked in, here is how to get out. Domain transfer: Ask your developer to

Hosting migration: If your site is on a standard platform (WordPress, Gatsby, etc.), set up a new hosting account in your name, deploy the site there, and update your domain's DNS to point to the new host. sourceMaterial.title: website redesign checklist
sourceMaterial.content: A website redesign for a small business should follow this checklist: audit your current traffic and rankings, preserve your existing SEO with 301 redirects, keep the content that already ranks, plan the new structure before building, test before launch, and measure the same metrics after. Skip any of these and you will lose traffic you spent years building. Redesigns fail when they treat the old site as disposable. Your current site has pages that rank, links that point to it, and traffic that comes from search. A redesign that ignores all of that is not an improvement. It is a reset. This checklist prevents that. If you want help with a redesign, see my website redesign services or contact me to talk about your specific site. Step 1: Audit your current site Before you change anything,

sourceMaterial.content: you need to know what you have. An audit tells you what is working so you do not throw it away. Traffic audit Connect Google Analytics and Google Search Console if you have not already Record your average monthly visitors for the last 12 months Note your top 10 pages by traffic Note your top 10 landing pages (the pages people enter through) Record your bounce rate and average session duration Write these numbers down. You will compare them after the redesign. Ranking audit In Search Console, export the list of queries that bring traffic to your site Note which pages rank for which queries Record your average position for your top 20 queries Check if any pages rank on page 1 of Google. Those pages are assets. Do not delete them. Content audit List every page on your current site For each

Those pages have SEO value. If you are going to change the URL of a page with backlinks, you need a 301 redirect. Step 2: Preserve your SEO This is the step most redesigns skip. If you do nothing else on this list, do this. 301 redirects Every old URL that has traffic, rankings, or backlinks needs a 301 redirect to the most relevant new URL. A 301 redirect tells search engines "this page has permanently moved" and passes most of the

Map every old URL to a new URL in a spreadsheet before you build If a page is being removed, redirect it to the closest equivalent, not the homepage Test every redirect after launch. A broken redirect is worse than no redirect. Keep the content that ranks If a page ranks on page 1 for a keyword, keep the core content. You can redesign the layout, update the design, and improve the formatting. Do not rewrite the text from scratch. Search engines ranked that text for a reason. Keep the heading structure (H1, H2, H3) if it is working Keep the keyword usage in titles and meta descriptions Keep the word count similar or longer Update outdated information but do not strip the substance Preserve your XML sitemap Generate a new sitemap after the redesign Submit it to

Only change if there is a real reason. Not testing on mobile. Most of your traffic is mobile. If it is broken on a phone, it is broken. Launching on a Friday and not checking until Monday. sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: Above the fold on a small business website you need five things: what you do, who it is for, where you work, what it costs, and what to do next. If a visitor sees those five things in the first screen without scrolling, they have enough information to decide whether to keep reading or contact you. If any one is missing, they scroll or they leave. "Above the fold" comes from newspapers. The stories visible when the paper was folded on a newsstand were the ones that sold the paper. On a website, it means what a visitor sees before they scroll. On a phone, that is roughly 600 800 pixels of vertical space. Not much room. Every element has to earn its place. Here are the five things that belong there, why each one matters, and what happens when it is missing. What should the headline say above

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: the fold? Your headline should be one sentence that says what your business does and where you do it. Use the formula [what you do] + [where you do it], such as "Plumbing repairs and installations in Durand, IL." Avoid taglines, mission statements, and generic phrases like "Quality service you can trust." Keep it under 12 words so a visitor knows they are in the right place within two seconds. This is the headline. One sentence that says what your business does. Not a tagline, not a mission statement, not "Welcome to our website." Why it matters: A visitor who lands on your site from a search result or a referral link has no context. They need to know in the first 2 seconds whether they are in the right place. If they cannot tell what you do, they go back to the search results. Good:

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: "Plumbing repairs and installations in Durand, IL." Bad: "Quality service you can trust since 1987." The first one tells you exactly what the business does and where. The second one tells you nothing. "Quality service" could be anything. A plumber, a mechanic, a cleaning service, a restaurant. How to write it: Use the formula [what you do] + [where you do it]. "HVAC repair and installation in Rock County, Wisconsin." "Roofing and gutters in Winnebago County." Keep it under 12 words. Who should the above the fold content target? Your above the fold content should tell visitors who you serve so the right ones self select and the wrong ones move on. Add "for homeowners," "for small businesses," or "for renters and landlords" to your headline or subheadline. If you try to speak to everyone,

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: you speak to no one. Being specific saves everyone time. Not every visitor is your customer. A residential plumber does not need commercial property managers calling them. A wedding photographer does not need corporate event inquiries. Telling people who you serve helps the right visitors self select and the wrong visitors move on. Why it matters: If you try to speak to everyone, you speak to no one. A headline that says "Plumbing repairs for homeowners in Durand, IL" tells a homeowner they are in the right place and tells a commercial property manager they should look elsewhere. That saves everyone time. Good: "Plumbing repairs for homeowners in Durand, IL and surrounding areas." Bad: "Plumbing solutions for all your needs." How to write it: Add who you serve to your headline or

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: subheadline. "for homeowners," "for small businesses," "for renters and landlords." Be specific. Should I list my service area above the fold? Yes, list your service area above the fold. Local search is about geography — if a visitor cannot tell whether you serve their area, they will not contact you. List the specific cities or counties you serve, or state your service radius, such as "Within 30 miles of Durand, IL." Do not be vague with phrases like "serving the Midwest." Local search is about geography. If a visitor cannot tell whether you serve their area, they will not contact you. This is especially important if you serve a specific region rather than a whole state. Why it matters: A visitor in Beloit, WI who finds a plumber in Durand, IL needs to know if that plumber drives to

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: Beloit. If the site does not say, the visitor assumes no and leaves. If the site says "serving Durand, Davis, Rockford, and Beloit," the visitor knows they are covered. Good: "Serving Durand, Davis, Rockford, and Beloit areas." Bad: No mention of service area, or "serving the Midwest." How to write it: List the cities or counties you actually serve. If you have a service radius, say so: "Within 30 miles of Durand, IL." Do not be vague. If you only work in one county, say one county. Should I show pricing above the fold? Yes, show at least a starting price or range above the fold. Price is a qualifier — visitors want to know if they can afford you before they pick up the phone. If they see no price, they assume it is expensive and leave. A simple "Service calls start at $89" or "Free

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: estimates on installations" filters out people who cannot afford you and encourages those who can. This is the one most small businesses skip. They do not want to list prices because they want to have a conversation first. I understand the reasoning, but it creates friction. Visitors want to know if they can afford you before they pick up the phone. Why it matters: Price is a qualifier. If a visitor sees that a service call is $89, they know whether that fits their budget. If they see no price, they assume it is expensive and leave. Listing even a starting price or a range filters out people who cannot afford you and encourages people who can. Good: "Service calls start at $89. Free estimates on installations." Bad: "Call for pricing." or no mention of cost at all. How to write it: You do

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: not need to list every price. A starting price, a range, or a "starting at" figure is enough. If you offer free estimates, say so. If you have different tiers, list them. See my pricing page for an example of transparent pricing. What call to action belongs above the fold? Pick one primary action and make it a button with action oriented text: "Call Now," "Request a Free Estimate," or "Book Online." Do not offer multiple competing CTAs — that reduces the chance of any action being taken. Make the button a contrasting color so it stands out. A clear single CTA gives the visitor an obvious next step. The call to action. After a visitor reads what you do, who you serve, where you work, and what it costs, they need to know what to do next. If there is no clear next step, they do nothing. They

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: might bookmark the page. They usually leave. Why it matters: A clear CTA gives the visitor a single, obvious action to take. "Call now," "Request a quote," "Book online." One action, not three. Multiple CTAs compete with each other and reduce the chance of any action being taken. Good: A button that says "Call (608) 313-5373" or "Request a Free Estimate." Bad: Three buttons: "Learn More," "About Us," "Contact." No clear primary action. How to write it: Pick one primary action and make it a button. Use action text, not generic text. "Call Now" is better than "Click Here." "Get a Free Estimate" is better than "Submit." Make the button a contrasting color so it stands out. How does above the fold change on mobile? On mobile, above the fold is roughly 600 800 pixels — less than half of a

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: desktop screen. Prioritize the headline and the call to action, since those two must be visible. Put the service area and pricing in a smaller subheadline below the main headline. Use a single column layout and test on an actual phone, not just a resized browser window. Above the fold on mobile is roughly 600 800 pixels. Less than half of a desktop screen. What to do: Prioritize the headline and the CTA. Those two must be visible. The service area and pricing can go in a smaller subheadline below the main headline. Use a single column layout. Do not try side by side elements on mobile. Test on an actual phone. A browser at 375px width is not the same as a real device. What does a good vs bad above the fold layout look like? A bad layout uses a rotating image slider, a generic "Welcome"

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: headline, multiple competing buttons, and no phone number, service area, or pricing. A good layout uses one static compressed hero image, a specific headline like "Plumbing Repairs for Homeowners in Durand, IL," a subheadline with pricing, and one clear call to action button. The good layout tells a visitor everything in one screen. Bad layout: Full width slider with 5 rotating images "Welcome to Smith Plumbing" headline Three buttons: Home, Services, About No phone number, service area, or pricing visible Good layout: One static hero image (compressed, under 200KB) Headline: "Plumbing Repairs for Homeowners in Durand, IL" Subheadline: "Same day service available. Service calls start at $89." One button: "Call (608) 313-5373" Phone number visible in header on every page The good layout

sourceMaterial.title: what belongs above the fold
sourceMaterial.content: tells a visitor everything they need to know in one screen and gives them one clear action to take. What is the bottom line on above the fold content? Above the fold is not about fitting as much as possible into one screen. It is about fitting the right five things: what you do, who it is for, where you work, what it costs, and what to do next. Get those five right and the rest of your page can provide detail. Get them wrong and no one scrolls down to see the rest. If you want a homepage that gets these five things right, my small business web design service builds pages designed to convert visitors into calls. Or reach out directly and I will look at what you have.

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: A five page business website needs a Home page, an About page, a Services page, a Contact page, and one social proof page (Testimonials or Case Studies). Each page has one job. The Home page gets people to other pages. The About page builds trust. The Services page explains what you do. The Contact page makes it easy to reach you. The social proof page closes the deal. Most small business websites fail because they try to do too much on each page or too little across all of them. A five page site is not a limitation. It is a structure. When each page has a clear purpose, the site converts better than a 20 page site where nothing is findable. See small business web design services or use the contact page to talk about your site. Page 1: Home The Home page is not a welcome mat. It is a

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: routing page. Its job is to answer three questions in under 10 seconds: who you are, what you do, and who you do it for. Then it gets people to the right page. What goes on the Home page A headline that says what you do. Not "Welcome to our website." Something like "Plumbing repairs and installations in Winnebago County." A subheadline that says who you serve. "Residential and commercial plumbing for Rockford and surrounding areas." A primary call to action. One button. "Get a quote" or "Call now." Not three buttons competing for attention. Three to five service summaries with links to Services. Short descriptions, not full paragraphs. One trust signal. A short testimonial, a badge, or "Serving Illinois since 2012." A footer with your NAP. Name, address, phone number. This matters for

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: local SEO. What to avoid A full company history. That goes on About. Every service you offer in detail. That goes on Services. A carousel slider. They slow down the page and nobody clicks past the first slide. Stock photos of handshakes. Use real photos or none. Page 2: About The About page is where trust gets built. People hire people they trust, and the About page is where they decide if they trust you. It is not a resume. It is a story about why you do what you do and who you are. What goes on the About page Who you are. A real photo, not a stock image. Your name and role. Why you started the business. Two or three sentences. People connect with motivation. Your credentials and experience. Keep it relevant. "Licensed Illinois plumber, 15 years experience" matters more than your high

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: school. Your service area. Be specific. "Durand, Rockford, Freeport, and surrounding areas." A personal detail. Not a full bio, but enough to feel like a real person. What to avoid Writing in third person if you are a solo business. "Bradley Matera is a web developer" sounds like a press release. "I build websites" sounds like a person. Listing every job you have ever had. Keep it to what is relevant. A wall of text with no headings. Break it up. Page 3: Services The Services page is the most important page for conversion. It is where someone decides if you do what they need. Be specific. Vague service descriptions lose customers. What goes on the Services page Each service as its own section with a heading. "Drain cleaning," "Water heater installation," "Emergency repairs." Not just

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: "Plumbing services." What is included in each service. Bullet points. People scan. What it costs, or a range. If you can list prices, do it. If not, say "Contact for pricing" and explain why (materials vary, scope varies). A call to action after each service. "Get a quote for drain cleaning" linking to the Contact page. FAQs if you get the same questions repeatedly. "Do you offer emergency service?" "Do you charge for estimates?" What to avoid One paragraph that says "We offer a full range of plumbing services." That tells the customer nothing. Hiding your most popular service at the bottom. Put it first. No call to action. Every service section should have a next step. If you have more than 5 services, consider splitting Services into separate pages. But for a five page site, one Services

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: page with clear sections works. Page 4: Contact The Contact page should be the easiest page on your site to use. If someone has to think about how to reach you, you have already lost them. What goes on the Contact page A contact form. Keep it short. Name, email or phone, message. Do not ask for their company size, budget, and project timeline on a contact form for a plumbing business. Your phone number. Clickable on mobile. This is the most important element for local businesses. Your email address. Not just a form. Some people want to email. Your physical address with an embedded map. This helps local SEO and helps customers find you. Your hours. Be honest. If you do not answer the phone after 5 PM, say so. Your service area listed in text. Search engines read text, not maps. What to

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: avoid A form with 10 required fields. Three is enough. No phone number. For local businesses, the phone number is the primary conversion. A CAPTCHA that is impossible to pass. Use a simple spam filter. Page 5: Testimonials or Case Studies The fifth page is social proof. You have two options: a Testimonials page or a Case Studies page. Pick one based on your business type. Testimonials page (for service businesses) 5 to 10 real testimonials with customer names and locations A mix of specific and general. "Fixed my burst pipe in 30 minutes on a Sunday" is better than "Great service." Photos of the customer or the work if you have permission A link to your Google reviews if you have them Case Studies page (for B2B or project based businesses) 3 to 5 detailed case studies The problem, the

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: solution, and the result for each Real numbers if you have them. "Reduced load time from 4.2s to 0.8s." Photos or screenshots of the work What to avoid on either Fake testimonials. People can tell. One line reviews with no context. "Awesome job!" does not sell anything. No names. "A satisfied customer" is not a testimonial. How the pages connect A five page site works when the pages link to each other intentionally. The Home page links to Services. The Services page links to Contact. The About page links to Testimonials. The Contact page references the service area from the About page. Every page should have one primary call to action. On Home, it is "view services." On Services, it is "get a quote." On About, it is "see what clients say." On Testimonials, it is "contact us." On Contact,

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: it is the form itself. If you build this structure, your five page site will outperform most 20 page sites. Clarity beats volume. What NOT to include on a 5 page site A five page site is a discipline. The constraint is what makes it work. Here is what to cut: A blog. If you are not going to write regularly, an empty blog with three posts from 2023 makes your site look abandoned. Add a blog when you commit to posting monthly. A separate page for every service. If you offer five services, one Services page with five sections is better than five thin pages. Split them into separate pages only when you have enough distinct content to justify it. A photo gallery on its own page. Fold photos into the relevant page. A gallery page with no context does not convert. Social media feeds embedded on

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: the site. They slow down the page and they break when the platform changes its API. Link to your profiles instead. A "Links" or "Resources" page. Unless you are curating something genuinely useful, this is filler that dilutes your site. Pop ups and exit intent overlays. On a five page local business site, these annoy more than they convert. Put your call to action in the page content. How to expand beyond 5 pages when ready The right time to add pages is when you have content that deserves its own URL. Here is the order I recommend: 1. Individual service pages — when your Services page is getting too long or when a specific service has enough detail (pricing, process, FAQs) to fill a page. This also helps with SEO because each page can target a specific service keyword. 2. A blog — when

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: you will commit to posting at least monthly. Blog posts are how you capture long tail search traffic and answer customer questions before they call. 3. Location landing pages — when you serve multiple cities and want to rank in each one. Each page needs unique content, not just a city name swap. I cover this in my local SEO services. 4. A case study or project portfolio — when you have enough completed work to show real results with specifics. 5. An FAQ page — when you are answering the same five questions over the phone. Move them to a page and link to it from your contact page. Add pages one at a time. A site that grows from 5 to 8 pages over a year is healthier than a site that launches with 15 pages of thin content. Common mistakes on small websites The mistakes I see most often on

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: five page sites: Writing for search engines instead of customers. Keyword stuffed headings like "Plumber Rockford IL Drain Cleaning Rockford" make your site read like a spam email. Write naturally. Search engines are smart enough. No phone number above the fold. On mobile, if a customer has to scroll to find your number, you lose calls. Put it in the header. Using stock photos that look like stock photos. A photo of a smiling customer service representative with a headset is a red flag. Use real photos of your work, your team, or your location. If you do not have real photos, use clean design instead. No call to action on the Services page. People read about your services and then... nothing. Every service section should link to Contact. An About page written in corporate speak. "Our

sourceMaterial.title: what five page website should include
sourceMaterial.content: mission is to deliver excellence." Nobody reads that. Write like you talk. Forgetting to test on a phone. More than half of local search traffic is mobile. If your site looks bad on a phone, you are losing customers. Examples of effective 5 page small business sites I will not link to specific client sites here, but I can describe what works. A plumber in Rockford runs a five page site: Home with a headline and three service links, About with a real photo and service area, Services broken into five clear sections with pricing ranges, Contact with a clickable number and embedded map, and a Testimonials page with eight real reviews pulled from Google. The site ranks in the local pack and gets 20 30 calls a month from organic search. It is not fancy. It is clear. A salon in Springfield runs a

sourceMaterial.content: similar structure but swaps Testimonials for a Case Studies page showing before and after photos of work. The Contact page lists hours, address, and a booking link. No blog, no gallery, no fluff. The site converts because every page has one job and does it. The pattern is the same: clear headline, real photos, specific services, easy contact, social proof. That is what a five page site should do. Want this built for you? I build five page business websites starting at $447. See small business web design or contact me to talk about your project.

sourceMaterial.title: why visitors leave local business website
sourceMaterial.content: Most visitors leave a local business website because it loads slowly, does not say what the business does in the first few seconds, is hard to use on a phone, makes contact difficult, or gives no reason to trust the business. Fix those five things and bounce rates drop. This post covers the seven most common reasons and how to fix each one. I have looked at a lot of small business websites. Most of them lose visitors for the same handful of reasons. It is rarely one big thing. It is usually a combination of small friction points that add up to someone hitting the back button before they ever pick up the phone. Here are the seven reasons I see most often, and what to do about each one. Why does a slow website make visitors leave? If your site takes more than 3 seconds to load on a phone, a

sourceMaterial.title: why visitors leave local business website
sourceMaterial.content: significant chunk of visitors are gone before they see anything. A 5MB hero image, multiple tracking scripts, and uncompressed images all add load time. Compressing images to under 200KB, removing unused scripts, and enabling lazy loading can cut load time from 6 seconds to 2 seconds and drop bounce rates by 27 points. This is the number one reason. If your site takes more than 3 seconds to load on a phone, a significant chunk of visitors are gone before they see anything. What it looks like: A homepage with a 5MB hero image, three tracking scripts, and a slider that loads all images at once. The visitor stares at a white screen. How to fix it: Compress images before uploading. A hero image does not need to be 5MB. Aim for under 200KB. Remove scripts you do not need. Every analytics tool,

sourceMaterial.title: why visitors leave local business website
sourceMaterial.content: chat widget, and tracking pixel adds load time. Use lazy loading for images below the fold. Before: 6.2 second load time on mobile, 68% bounce rate. After: 2.1 second load time, bounce rate dropped to 41%. If your site is slow, start with my website speed optimization service. Speed is the foundation everything else sits on. Why do visitors leave when they cannot tell what you do? Visitors should know what you do, who you serve, and where you work within the first screen. If your homepage starts with "Welcome to our website!" and a photo of a building, they have to scroll to figure out what business they are looking at — and most will not. A one sentence headline like "Plumbing repairs in Durand, IL — same day service available" tells them immediately. Visitors should know what you do, who

sourceMaterial.title: why visitors leave local business website
sourceMaterial.content: you serve, and where you work within the first screen. If they have to scroll to figure out what business they are looking at, they leave. What it looks like: A homepage that starts with "Welcome to our website!" and a photo of a building. No mention of what the business actually does until the third paragraph. How to fix it: Put a one sentence headline at the top that says what you do and for whom. Example: "Plumbing repairs and installations in Durand, Illinois and surrounding areas." Do not make people guess. Tell them. Before: "Welcome to Smith Plumbing Family Owned Since 1987" After: "Plumbing Repairs in Durand, IL Same Day Service Available" The second one tells you what they do, where they work, and gives a reason to act now. If your site has text too small to read without pinching, buttons too close together to tap, horizontal scrolling, or forms that are painful on a touchscreen, you are losing most of your potential customers. Use 16px font sizes, 44x44 pixel tap targets, and mobile optimized form inputs to fix it. Over 60% of local business website traffic comes from phones.
